TL;DR: The paper introduces IR3DE, a Ridge Regression-based inference router for selecting appropriate domain-expert LLMs for tasks, achieving competitive results with low cost and fast decision-making.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for efficient routing methods to select the best-suited LLMs for various tasks, addressing limitations of existing methods that are either costly or require significant retraining.

Method: IR3DE utilizes Ridge Regression to provide quick routing decisions without the need for extensive training, allowing dynamic adjustment of the set of domain expert LLMs.

Result: IR3DE achieves performance near existing baselines in Causal Language Modeling tasks and outperforms them in reasoning tasks, achieving a normalized performance score of 98.4%.

Conclusion: IR3DE offers a scalable solution for integrating domain expert LLMs, enabling quick adjustments without full retraining.

Abstract: Foundational Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate proficiency on a wide range of general tasks, and achieve remarkable results on various specialized tasks via domain-expert LLMs. With the ever-growing list of available LLMs, inference routers are being proposed to select the most appropriate LLM for each prompt. However, existing routing methods either optimize cost across weak-to-strong generalist LLMs or require substantial training to support domain-expertise routing. In this paper, we propose IR3DE, a Ridge Regression-based Router for Domain Experts that provides cheap and fast routing decisions for each prompt. We evaluate IR3DE in two Causal Language Modeling (CLM) settings where the tasks are next-token prediction for all domains, and one reasoning setting where each domain has its own distinct reasoning task. Despite being a linear router, IR3DE achieves performance comparable to the other baselines in both CLM settings, and surpassing them in the reasoning setting, with a normalized performance of 98.4%. Moreover, IR3DE enables the addition or removal of new domain experts without requiring the router to be retrained from scratch, allowing a dynamic set of LLMs to be served with minimal disruption to the router itself. Our code is available at: github.com/gensyn-ai/IR3DE.

</details>


### [183] [Harnessing Structural Context for Entity Alignment Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06109)
*Xingyu Chen,Yuanning Cui,Zequn Sun,Wei Hu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ContextEA improves entity alignment (EA) by leveraging structural contexts for better performance across heterogeneous knowledge graphs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enhance the effectiveness of currently used EA models, which underuse structural contexts during encoding and candidate ranking processes.

Method: ContextEA introduces a cross-KG interaction encoder for improved relation-aware propagation, and a structural calibration decoder that uses various levels of structural evidence for alignment score calibration.

Result: Experiments on 29 EA datasets show ContextEA outperforms strong baselines, with pretrained models surpassing finetuned ones across all benchmarks, indicating superior transferability to unseen KGs.

Conclusion: Harnessing structural context significantly enhances EA foundation models, proving to be a promising approach for knowledge graph integration.

Abstract: Entity alignment (EA) aims to identify equivalent entities across heterogeneous knowledge graphs (KGs) and is a key component of knowledge fusion and cross-KG reasoning. The recent EA foundation model demonstrates that alignment knowledge, once pretrained, can be directly applied to diverse previously unseen KG pairs. However, it still underuses structural context in two places: cross-KG interaction is weak during encoding, and final candidate ranking still relies too heavily on coarse similarity. We address these limitations with ContextEA, an enhanced encoder-decoder framework for transferable EA. On the encoder side, we introduce a cross-KG interaction encoder that unifies the two KGs with anchor bridges and performs earlier relation-aware cross-graph propagation. On the decoder side, we introduce a structural calibration decoder that calibrates alignment scores with entity-level, neighborhood-level, relation-level, and anchor-aware structural evidence. This design strengthens both structural context construction and structural context exploitation while remaining lightweight. Experiments on 29 EA datasets in OpenEA, SRPRS, and DBP show consistent gains over strong transferable baselines. Notably, the pretrained ContextEA already surpasses the finetuned baselines on all three benchmark groups, demonstrating substantially stronger transfer to unseen KGs. These results suggest that explicitly harnessing structural context is an effective direction for improving EA foundation models.

</details>


### [184] [Ouvia: A User-centered Framework for Measuring Usability of Speech Translation in Real-World Communication Scenarios](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06177)
*Giuseppe Attanasio,Beatrice Savoldi,Daniel Chechelnitsky,Matteo Negri,Marine Carpuat,Maarten Sap,André F. T. Martins*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Ouvia is a framework for evaluating user-perceived usability in speech translation for one-to-one communication, revealing significant usability gaps and the importance of demographic considerations in real-world applications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper aims to address the inadequacy of existing ST evaluation methods, which ignore user communication needs in real-world contexts.

Method: The authors developed Ouvia, a framework tested through a web app that gathered over 1,750 interactions in diverse settings, assessing usability across various speech translation systems and user demographics.

Result: Findings indicate that only about 50% of interactions are considered usable, with notable usability disparities among different demographic groups. QA-based evaluation outperformed standard quality metrics in predicting usability.

Conclusion: The study emphasizes the necessity for user-centered evaluation frameworks that prioritize contextual usability and reflect the actual experiences of diverse user groups.

Abstract: Speech translation (ST) is increasingly adopted in user applications, yet its evaluation largely focuses on decontextualized testbeds and holistic quality, rather than end users' communication needs. We introduce Ouvia, an evaluation framework for measuring user-perceived usability of speech translation outputs in real-world settings. Ouvia focuses on one-to-one communication: an English speaker needs to convey a request to a Portuguese speaker, and the message is automatically translated. Through a custom web app and multi-phase study design, we collect more than 1,750 such interactions in healthcare and everyday situations, mediated by four ST systems, involving speakers from three English dialects and two genders. We find that modern ST serves people only to a limited extent -- only around half of interactions are rated as usable -- with significant gaps in reported usability across demographic groups. Moreover, among quality metrics, we find that QA-based evaluation is a substantially stronger predictor of real-world usability than standard approaches. Together, these findings stress the importance of situated, user-centered evaluation frameworks that go beyond holistic quality scores and attend to who the technology serves -- and how well.

</details>


### [185] [The Tell-Tale Norm: $\ell_2$ Magnitude as a Signal for Reasoning Dynamics in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06188)
*Jinyang Zhang,Hongxin Ding,Yue Fang,Weibin Liao,Muyang Ye,Junfeng Zhao,Yasha Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper explores the l2 norm of hidden states in Large Language Models (LLMs) as a signal for layer-wise reasoning dynamics, proposing techniques to enhance reasoning performance based on this insight.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To identify a model-intrinsic signal that captures the reasoning dynamics of LLMs, particularly through layer-wise analysis.

Method: The authors analyze the l2 norm of hidden states in LLMs using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), establishing a link between reasoning intensity and latent geometry and validating their findings through empirical correlation and causal interventions.

Result: The study finds that a sharp increase in reasoning feature activations occurs in late layers of LLMs, and demonstrates that the l2 norm correlates positively with important reasoning steps; new techniques are introduced that improve reasoning performance without requiring additional training.

Conclusion: The l2 norm of hidden states serves as a simple and effective tool for understanding and enhancing reasoning dynamics in LLMs, benefiting various model architectures and benchmarks.

Abstract: Recent work has sought to understand Large Language Models (LLMs) reasoning, yet a principled, model-intrinsic signal that captures its layer-wise reasoning dynamics remains underexplored. We bridge this gap by demonstrating that the l2 norm of hidden states serves as an endogenous signal of the model's reasoning intensity. Using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) as a diagnostic probe, we observe that LLMs' internal reasoning is marked by a sharp increase in reasoning feature activations concentrated in late layers. Motivated by this pattern, we establish a formal link between reasoning intensity and the model's latent geometry and theoretically prove that the l2 norm of hidden states bounds the activation strength of SAE reasoning features. Empirical correlation analysis and causal interventions further validate the l2 norm as a faithful indicator, where heightened norms consistently correspond to critical reasoning steps. We then introduce three test-time scaling techniques guided by l2 norms: (i) Adaptive Layer-wise Reasoning Recursion, (ii) Endogenous Reasoning State Steering, and (iii) l2-guided Response Selection, which requires no additional training or data and is compatible with advanced inference engines. Experiments across model architectures and benchmarks show that l2-norm-based techniques significantly improve reasoning performance, offering a principled yet simple lens to perceive and control LLM latent reasoning dynamics. Our code is available at https://github.com/zjy1298/The-Tell-Tale-Norm.

</details>


### [186] [Improving Answer Extraction in Context-based Question Answering Systems Using LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06197)
*Hafez Abdelghaffar,Ahmed Alansary,Ali Hamdi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper presents a refined question answering system utilizing large language models to enhance answer accuracy and relevance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the limitations of existing QA systems, particularly their inaccuracies with complex queries despite having access to relevant contexts.

Method: Fine-tuning a pre-trained LLM (Roberta-base) on the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD1.1) to enhance contextual understanding and answer extraction.

Result: The fine-tuned Roberta-base model achieves ROUGE-L of 86.84%, BLEU score of 28.24%, and BERTScore of 95.38%, indicating improved accuracy and relevance in answer production.

Conclusion: Targeted fine-tuning significantly enhances the reliability and precision of question answering systems.

Abstract: Question answering (QA) systems have achieved notable progress with the advent of large language models (LLMs). However, they still face challenges in accurately extracting and generating precise answers from given contexts, particularly when dealing with complex or ambiguous queries. Existing approaches often struggle with contextual understanding, answer consistency, and generalization across diverse domains. In this work, we propose a question answering system based on large language models, where the input consists of a textual context and a corresponding question, and the output is a concise and accurate answer. The motivation behind this research lies in addressing the limitations of current QA systems, particularly their tendency to produce irrelevant or imprecise responses despite having access to the correct context. Our methodology involves fine-tuning a pre-trained LLM on a benchmark QA dataset to improve its contextual comprehension and answer extraction capabilities. Specifically, we utilize the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD1.1), which provides high-quality context-question-answer triplets for supervised training and evaluation. Experimental results show that the fine-tuned Roberta-base model achieves the highest performance, attaining a ROUGE-L score of 86.84%, a BLEU score of 28.24%, and a BERTScore of 95.38%. These results indicate strong accuracy and answer relevance, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach for context-based question answering tasks. Furthermore, the findings confirm that targeted fine-tuning substantially improves the reliability and precision of QA systems.

</details>


### [187] [Dense Contexts Are Hard Contexts: Lexical Density Limits Effective Context in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06203)
*Giovanni Dettori,Matteo Boffa,Danilo Giordano,Idilio Drago,Marco Mellia*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Lexical density significantly impacts the performance of LLMs in long-context tasks, revealing a potential reduction in effective context capacity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate lexical density as a key factor affecting LLM performance in long-context scenarios, in addition to input length and information position.

Method: The study employs three benchmarks with identical token length and controlled information position but varies lexical density to assess its impact on retrieval performance of various LLMs.

Result: Higher lexical density leads to a sharp decline in model performance, with retrieval scores dropping below 60% in dense contexts compared to near-perfect scores in sparse contexts.

Conclusion: Lexical density is crucial in determining LLM effective context capacity, which should be considered in the design and applications of real-world LLM systems.

Abstract: Input length and the position of relevant information are widely cited as the primary causes of degraded LLM long-context performance. Here, we study lexical density -- the rate at which a context introduces distinct information -- as a third, largely overlooked factor that systematically reduces the effective context window of LLMs. We quantify the impact of lexical density on open-weight LLMs (9B-685B) using three "find-the-needle" style benchmarks with identical length (~12k tokens) and controlled needle position, but increasing density of information. We observe a sharp performance collapse in higher-density benchmarks: models that are near-perfect in sparse contexts drop below 60% retrieval score on denser ones. To rule out task-type confounds, we vary and control the density within each benchmark while keeping all other properties unchanged. Reducing density generally restores performance, especially in the high-density regimes where degradation appears. These results show that effective context capacity is a function of lexical density, with direct implications for real-world LLM systems operating on compact, information-rich inputs.

</details>


### [188] [FiLM-Based Speaker Conditioning of a SpeechLLM for Pathological Speech Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06211)
*Fernando López,Santosh Kesiraju,Jordi Luque*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper explores improving automatic speech recognition (ASR) for pathological speech using Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) to adapt a frozen ASR model without altering its weights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the challenges faced in ASR for pathological speech, which is underrepresented in current technologies.

Method: Utilizing FiLM to inject speaker-specific x-vector information into each transformer layer of a frozen ASR encoder, allowing adaptation to individual pathological speakers.

Result: The speaker-conditioned ASR showed competitive performance against other adaptation strategies and maintained its effectiveness on non-conditioned speech.

Conclusion: The proposed method enhances ASR for pathological speech while preserving performance on standard speech tasks.

Abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) has advanced remarkably for standard speech; however, pathological speech from neurological conditions remains a significant challenge. We investigate speaker conditioning via Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM), injecting x-vector-derived information into each transformer layer of a frozen ASR encoder to adapt internal representations to individual pathological speakers without modifying base model weights. We benchmark this for the ASR task against standard and parameter-efficient fine-tuning baselines, complemented by post-processing, on Spanish and English pathological speech. Additionally, we evaluate if the adapted model preserves the ability to answer speech-related questions. Results show that speaker-conditioned ASR is competitive with established adaptation strategies while retaining performance on non-conditioned speech.

</details>


### [189] [From Self to Other: Evaluating Demographic Perspective-Taking in LLM Hate Speech Annotation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06266)
*Paloma Piot,Javier Parapar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This study evaluates the effectiveness of persona-conditioned Large Language Models in simulating diverse opinions for hate speech detection, finding mixed performance across models and highlighting the potential of vicarious prompting with Llama 3.1.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the challenges of subjectivity in hate speech detection caused by differing demographic perceptions and the difficulties in obtaining diverse annotations at scale.

Method: The study assesses models on three dimensions: inter-group disagreement, in-group sensitivity, and vicarious prediction, using various persona-conditioned models to ascertain their capabilities in reflecting human-like judgment.

Result: No model consistently performed well across all dimensions; however, Llama 3.1 with vicarious prompting showed the highest agreement across demographic groups.

Conclusion: Vicarious prompting with Llama 3.1 could provide a more reliable method for automatic annotation that aligns better with human perceptions of hate speech.

Abstract: Hate speech detection is inherently subjective: people from different demographic groups perceive the same content very differently. Collecting enough annotations from multiple demographic groups is costly and difficult to scale. Persona-conditioned Large Language Models (models prompted to adopt a specific demographic identity) have been proposed as a way to simulate diverse perspectives at scale. But do they actually reflect how different groups disagree? We evaluate three aspects of human social judgement: (i) whether personas from different groups disagree in human-like ways (inter-group disagreement), (ii) whether they become more sensitive when content targets their own identity (in-group sensitivity), and (iii) whether they can accurately predict how another group would react (vicarious prediction). Our results show that no model consistently captures all three dimensions, and performance is highly model-dependent and does not emerge reliably from minimal identity prompts alone. However, vicarious prompting with Llama 3.1 yields the highest cross-group agreement in most demographic axes and provides the closest overall approximation to human disagreement patterns, indicating that this configuration may provide a more reliable setting for automatic annotation aligned with human judgements.

</details>


### [190] [Many Circuits, One Mechanism: Input Variation and Evaluation Granularity in Circuit Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06267)
*Alireza Bayat Makou,Jingcheng Niu,Subhabrata Dutta,Iryna Gurevych*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This study challenges the assumption that structural differences in circuit discovery methods indicate distinct functional mechanisms by demonstrating that structurally diverse circuits can perform the same computation under varied input conditions, a phenomenon termed phantom specialization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate the validity of interpreting structural differences in circuits as evidence of unique functional mechanisms.

Method: The authors vary input statistics while keeping the task constant and analyze the performance of extracted circuits across different frequency bands using Pythia models. They extract 75 circuits and conduct edge-level evaluations and causal interchange interventions.

Result: Findings indicate that structurally distinct circuits perform identical computations, with core structures enabling broad performance across frequency bands and pointing to interchangeable internal representations.

Conclusion: Structural differences do not equate to distinct mechanisms; edge-level evaluation and cross-condition tests are necessary to reveal the true nature of these circuits.

Abstract: Circuit discovery methods identify subgraphs that explain specific model behaviors, and structural differences between discovered circuits are commonly interpreted as evidence of distinct mechanisms. We test this assumption by varying input statistics while holding the task fixed, and show that the resulting structural differences exhibit apparent specialization but do not correspond to functional differences, a pattern we term phantom specialization. Using Literal Sequence Copying across four token-frequency bands plus a control condition in five Pythia models (70M-1.4B), we extract 75 circuits and find that structurally distinct circuits implement the same computation: band-specific edges transfer broadly across bands, a core shared across most bands recovers at least 99% of circuit performance, and causal interchange interventions confirm that internal representations are interchangeable across frequency bands. Repeated extractions within the same frequency band further suggest that discovery algorithms sample from an equivalence class of valid subgraphs rather than recovering a unique mechanism. Standard evaluation practice obscures this pattern: source-level evaluation inflates apparent faithfulness, while edge-level evaluation reveals the many-to-one mapping from structure to function. Our results show that structural differences between circuits are not sufficient evidence for distinct mechanisms, and that exposing this requires edge-level evaluation and cross-condition transfer tests.

</details>


### [191] [FOXGLOVE: Understanding Goal-Oriented and Anchored Writing Feedback from Experts and LLMs on Argumentative Essays](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06271)
*Yijun Liu,Yifan Song,John Gallagher,Sarah Sterman,Tal August*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper introduces FOXGLOVE, a dataset comparing feedback from human instructors and large language models (LLMs) on twelfth-grade essays, revealing similarities in feedback distribution but differences in sentence focus and complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the lack of systematic comparisons between LLM and expert feedback in writing revision, focusing on key dimensions like goal-orientation and prioritization.

Method: The study involves analyzing a dataset of 2,340 feedback comments—696 from human instructors and 1,644 from LLMs—across 69 essays, with expert quality ratings provided for comparison.

Result: Findings indicate that while feedback distribution is similar, instructors and LLMs differ in specific sentence focus; LLMs generate more complex and longer feedback, receiving higher quality ratings overall, although partly due to length.

Conclusion: FOXGLOVE allows for a detailed comparison of human and LLM feedback, highlighting areas of alignment and divergence.

Abstract: While large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate writing feedback, there remains no systematic comparison of LLM and expert feedback on the dimensions that writing research identifies as central to revision: goal-orientation, anchoring to specific sentences, and prioritization. We introduce FOXGLOVE, a dataset of 696 feedback comments written by trained writing instructors on 69 twelfth-grade argumentative essays, paired with 1,644 comments generated from four frontier LLMs under a shared protocol, totaling 2,340 comments. We provide expert quality ratings on a subset of both instructor and LLM comments. We find that instructors and LLMs distribute feedback similarly across goals and essay positions, yet instructors and models diverge on the specific sentences on which to provide feedback. Additionally, we find that models tend to write more complex feedback and use fewer questions than instructors. LLM feedback also receives higher ratings on most dimensions of quality, as rated by instructors, but much of this advantage appears to be attributable to lengthier comments. FOXGLOVE enables systematic comparison of where human and LLM feedback align, diverge, and differ.

</details>


### [192] [LLMs Can Leak Training Data But Do They Want To? A Propensity-Aware Evaluation of Memorization in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06286)
*Gianluca Barmina,Peter Schneider-Kamp,Lukas Galke Poech*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper presents PropMe, a framework for evaluating memorization in language models, highlighting the distinction between adversarial and ordinary use cases. It introduces a metric transformation for creating propensity metrics and evaluates two models, Comma and DFM Decoder, finding that while models can reproduce training data under direct prompts, they do so infrequently in typical scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the inadequacy of existing memorization evaluations that primarily focus on adversarial conditions instead of ordinary usage of language models.

Method: The authors introduce the PropMe framework along with a metric transformation for creating propensity metrics. They utilize a lightweight tracing pipeline, SimpleTrace, to attribute model outputs to training data and compute various memorization metrics.

Result: The evaluation of two language models shows a significant gap between capabilities elicited through specific prompts versus general usage. Prefix-based attacks reveal stronger memorization than non-adversarial prompts, with overall low propensity scores observed across tests.

Conclusion: The study emphasizes the need for comprehensive memorization audits that include both worst-case extractability and typical leakage propensity to better understand the memorization behavior of language models.

Abstract: Large language models can reproduce training data, but existing memorization evaluations mostly measure whether models can be forced to do so, rather than whether they do so under ordinary use. We introduce PropMe, a propensity-aware framework for memorization evaluation that contrasts prefix-based capability attacks with non-adversarial evaluations. We propose a metric transformation that, applied to existing functions, allows to create propensity metrics. We further introduce SimpleTrace, a lightweight tracing pipeline built on infini-gram that deterministically attributes model generations to large-scale training corpora and computes verbatim, near-verbatim, and propensity-transformed memorization metrics. Evaluating two fully-open models: Comma and DFM Decoder on two datasets: Common Pile and Dynaword in two languages, we find a consistent gap between capability and propensity: prefix attacks elicit substantially stronger memorization signals than generic or dataset-specific prompts, while propensity scores remain low overall. Thus, the models can reveal training data when directly elicited, but rarely do so in more common non-adversarial settings. We also find that DFM Decoder, which is continually pre-trained from Comma, exhibits reduced memorization and memorization propensity for Common Pile, confirming that memorization capability can decrease when later training emphasizes partially different data. Our results suggest, and we encourage, that memorization audits should report both worst-case extractability and ordinary leakage propensity in order to have a more comprehensive view of this phenomenon.

</details>


### [193] [Decomposing Factual Sycophancy in Language Models: How Size and Instruction Tuning Shape Robustness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06306)
*Victor De Marez,Luna De Bruyne,Walter Daelemans*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes factual sycophancy in language models, highlighting the separate influences of truth preference and manipulation sensitivity, while using 56 models to explore how size and instruction tuning impact vulnerability to social pressure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the mechanisms behind factual sycophancy in language models and to provide a clearer framework for evaluating their robustness against social pressures.

Method: The authors decompose factual sycophancy into truth margin and manipulation sensitivity and evaluate 56 models with varying sizes and manipulation types to assess the effects of size and instruction tuning.

Result: Size largely governs vulnerability to factual sycophancy, but instruction tuning alters this effect; small instruction-tuned models may become less robust, while large ones typically become more robust.

Conclusion: Factual sycophancy is multi-faceted and evaluations should focus on channel-specific, manipulation-specific, and size-conditioned robustness instead of relying solely on flip rates.

Abstract: Factual sycophancy occurs when a language model abandons a correct, verifiable answer under social pressure. Because a flip occurs only when pressure toward a false answer exceeds the model's neutral preference for the truth, flip rates conflate two mechanisms: the strength of that baseline preference (truth margin), and how far pressure shifts it (manipulation sensitivity). We decompose factual sycophancy into these channels and use them to separate the effects of size and instruction tuning across 56 open-weight models spanning 0.3B-32B parameters and 13 manipulation types. We find that vulnerability is governed mainly by size, but instruction tuning changes how size acts: small instruction-tuned models can become less robust, whereas large instruction-tuned models usually become more robust. Instruction tuning primarily increases truth margin, but its behavioral effect depends on manipulation type. Scaling also changes the two channels differently: base models gain margin but become mildly more manipulation-sensitive, whereas instruction-tuned models gain margin faster and become less sensitive. Factual sycophancy is therefore not a single scalar property. Evaluations should report channel-specific, manipulation-specific, and size-conditioned robustness rather than flip rates alone.

</details>


### [194] ["Chi nas dal soch el sent de legn" -- Auditing Text Corpora for Lombard](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06349)
*Edoardo Signoroni,Pavel Rychlý*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The study audits Lombard language corpora, revealing poor data quality and bias favoring Western over Eastern varieties, underscoring the need for community-driven curation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the lack of high-quality NLP tools for under-resourced languages, focusing on Lombard as a case study.

Method: A manual audit of parallel and monolingual corpora for Lombard to assess data quality and orthographic diversity.

Result: Identification of severe misidentification, noise in datasets, and a bias towards Western Lombard in high-quality data.

Conclusion: Emphasizes the necessity of community involvement for variety-aware data curation, rather than relying solely on quantity.

Abstract: Several of the world's languages are still under-resourced in terms of Natural Language Processing (NLP) tools. This is mostly due to the lack of high-quality datasets to train, develop, and evaluate systems and models for several tasks, such as Machine Translation (MT). We conduct a manual audit of the parallel and monolingual corpora available for Lombard, an under-resourced language continuum from Italy. Our analysis reveals that the perceived abundance of web-scraped data is an illusion, with massive datasets plagued by severe language misidentification, boilerplate text, and non-linguistic noise. Furthermore, we analyze the orthographic composition of the valid Lombard portions across web-scraped datasets, curated corpora, and benchmarks. Our findings show conflicting orthographical systems and severe representational bias across all corpora: high-quality data is heavily skewed towards Western Lombard varieties, with Eastern ones left on the margins. This underscores the need for variety-aware, community-driven data curation rather than purely quantity-driven scraping.

</details>


### [195] [EDIT: Evidence-Diagnosed Intervention Training for Rule-Faithful LLM Grading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06350)
*Zhihao Wu,Linhai Zhang,Taiyi Wang,Runcong Zhao,Peter Andrews,Cesare Aloisi,Yulan He*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Presenting EDIT, a two-phase framework that enhances rubric-aligned grading in LLMs by pinpointing and correcting flawed reasoning processes while using belief-informed reward structures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve rubric grading accuracy in LLMs by addressing the shortcomings of existing credit-assignment methods that fail to effectively diagnose and correct reasoning errors during assessment.

Method: EDIT consists of two phases: EDIT-SFT locates malfunctioning reasoning steps through internal model signals and revises them using a rubric checklist; EDIT-RL adjusts the grader's performance with belief-guided reward shaping to ensure model reliability.

Result: EDIT demonstrates superior performance over traditional fine-tuning and reinforcement learning methods in both in-domain and out-of-domain grading tasks, as shown in experiments and ablation studies.

Conclusion: The effectiveness of EDIT is attributed to its diagnostic capabilities that identify weaknesses in reasoning, leading to improved grading fidelity.

Abstract: Reliable rubric grading requires more than accurate score prediction. Each judgement must be grounded in the mark scheme and evidence from the student answer. Existing credit-assignment and intervention methods, primarily designed for self-contained reasoning tasks such as mathematics reasoning, struggle in this setting because they do not identify where grading reasoning goes wrong or how the model's belief about the final mark changes during reasoning. We propose Evidence-Diagnosed Intervention Training (EDIT), a two-phase framework for training more rubric-faithful LLM graders. First, EDIT-SFT locates problematic reasoning steps using internal model signals: posterior belief over the final mark and input-grounding scores. It then revises only these local steps with help from a rubric checklist. Second, EDIT-RL calibrates the grader with belief-guided reward shaping, penalising large harmful belief drifts while still allowing helpful exploration. Experiments on two real-world, multi-subject grading benchmarks demonstrate that EDIT consistently outperforms strong supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning baselines on both in-domain and out-of-domain splits, with ablation studies confirming that internal-state diagnostics drive these gains.

</details>


### [196] [CollabSim: A CSCW-Grounded Methodology for Investigating Collaborative Competence of LLM Agents through Controlled Multi-Agent Experiments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06399)
*Jiaju Chen,Bo Sun,Yuxuan Lu,Yun Wang,Dakuo Wang,Bingsheng Yao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces CollabSim, a framework for analyzing collaborative competence in multi-agent systems built on large language models, addressing their limitations in teamwork dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the gap in evaluating the collaborative competence of agents in multi-agent systems, motivated by findings that such systems falter due to poor collaboration rather than individual performance.

Method: CollabSim provides a configurable simulation framework with a theory-grounded definition of collaborative capabilities, manipulation of interaction conditions, and probing of agents' internal states during interactions.

Result: Experiments with four large language models demonstrate that CollabSim can effectively capture the effects of interaction conditions, distinguish model performance, and identify task-dependent impacts of agent design.

Conclusion: CollabSim offers a systematic approach to studying and improving the collaborative abilities of agents in multi-agent systems.

Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models have shown growing promise, with their effectiveness resting on agents' ability to coordinate through text-based channels much as human teams do. Yet recent study suggests that MAS often falter not because agents lack individual task-solving ability, but because they lack collaborative competence: the capacity to establish common ground, maintain shared task understanding, balance individual and collective incentives, and repair misalignment as interaction unfolds. Decades of research in Computer-Supported Cooperative Work have characterized these requirements for human teams coordinating under constrained communication, yet existing MAS evaluations focus mainly on task outcomes or single-agent proficiency in reasoning, planning, and tool use. To enable a systematic analysis of agents' collaborative competence in MAS, we introduce CollabSim, a configurable simulation framework that combines a theory-grounded definition of collaborative capabilities, controlled manipulation of interaction conditions, and action-level probing of agents' internal states. Experiments across four LLMs show that CollabSim can capture condition effects, separate model performance patterns, and reveal task-dependent effects of agent design.

</details>


### [197] [A Komi-Yazva--Russian Parallel Corpus and Evaluation Protocol for Zero- and Few-Shot LLM Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06420)
*Petr Parshakov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a Komi-Yazva-Russian parallel corpus and evaluation protocol for LLM translation in low-resource settings, revealing performance differences among models and prompting strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the translation challenges in endangered, low-resource languages using large language models.

Method: Analysis of 457 aligned sentence pairs in the Komi-Yazva-Russian corpus, applying zero-shot and retrieval-based few-shot prompting across various LLMs with comprehensive evaluation metrics.

Result: LLMs achieve non-trivial translation quality with significant performance variability by model and prompting regime, showing improved results in retrieval-based few-shot scenarios.

Conclusion: The study underscores the importance of metric choice and failure handling in evaluating endangered-language machine translation, presenting the corpus as a benchmarking resource.

Abstract: We present the first Komi-Yazva--Russian parallel corpus together with an explicit evaluation protocol for studying LLM translation in an endangered, extremely low-resource setting. The dataset contains 457 aligned sentence pairs from 74 narrative texts and is accompanied by documented provenance, sentence-level alignment, and story identifiers that enable leakage-aware evaluation. We use this setup to compare modern large language models on Komi-Yazva-to-Russian translation under severe parallel-data scarcity in zero-shot and retrieval-based few-shot regimes. The protocol includes story-level cross-validation, deterministic retrieval for few-shot prompting, strict validation of generated outputs, complementary reference-based and judge-based metrics, and story-level uncertainty estimates. Across models, LLMs produce non-trivial translations, but performance varies strongly by model family and prompting regime. Retrieval-based few-shot prompting consistently improves over zero-shot prompting, while gains beyond a small retrieved context remain limited. The results show that evaluative conclusions in this setting depend materially on metric choice and failure handling, so the paper frames the corpus as both a dataset contribution and a reproducible evaluation testbed for endangered-language machine translation.

</details>


### [198] [Reinforcement Learning Elicits Contextual Learning of Unseen Language Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06428)
*Hanxu Hu,Zdeněk Šnajdr,Pinzhen Chen,Jannis Vamvas,Rico Sennrich*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes a reinforcement learning approach for translating low-resource languages by leveraging in-context linguistic knowledge instead of memorization, showing improved outcomes over traditional methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous methods for translating low-resource languages struggle with overfitting and limited zero-shot transfer, leading to a need for LLMs to develop better in-context learning capabilities.

Method: The paper presents a reinforcement learning approach that utilizes a surface-level translation metric (chrF) as a reward signal to drive the learning process for translating unseen languages.

Result: The RL-trained models demonstrate superior performance in translating completely unseen languages compared to in-context learning and supervised fine-tuning, effectively utilizing linguistic context for better results.

Conclusion: The findings indicate that outcome-based reinforcement learning can be a valuable technique for enhancing language translation capabilities, extending its applicability beyond traditional reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Prior work has shown that large language models (LLMs) can translate unseen or low-resource languages by undergoing continued training or even by encoding a grammar book in their context. However, both methods typically overfit specific languages, with limited zero-shot transfer at test time. To translate extremely low-resource languages at scale, we argue that LLMs must acquire the meta-skill of utilizing in-context linguistic knowledge rather than memorizing specific languages. In this paper, we propose a reinforcement learning (RL) approach to unseen language translation given rich linguistic context, using a surface-level translation metric (chrF) as the reward. Empirically, despite the lightweight reward, our RL-trained models effectively extract and apply relevant linguistic information from the provided context, leading to better translations on completely unseen languages than in-context learning or supervised fine-tuning. Our analyses suggest that outcome-based RL can extend beyond conventional reasoning tasks like math and coding to serve as a recipe for language learning from context.

</details>


### [199] [Revising Context, Shifting Simulated Stance: Auditing LLM-Based Stance Simulation in Online Discussions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06443)
*Xinnong Zhang,Wanting Shan,Hanjia Lyu,Zhongyu Wei,Jiebo Luo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates the ability of large language models (LLMs) to simulate user stances in social media discussions, focusing on the impact of context changes on these simulations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To examine how changes in conversational contexts influence stance simulation accuracy in LLMs and to develop an evaluation framework for this purpose.

Method: The study employs counterfactual context revision strategies on original conversations to assess stance shifts using text-only and multimodal (meme-based) approaches, measuring their effectiveness through directional stance change and transition rate metrics.

Result: The findings demonstrate that both text-only and multimodal revision strategies lead to significant stance transitions, indicating the models' ability to reflect shifts based on contextual changes even under varied polarization mechanisms.

Conclusion: The research emphasizes the dual potential of LLMs in simulating online opinion dynamics, highlighting the necessity for careful consideration of context sensitivity in applications.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate social media users and infer how individuals may respond to online discussions. However, it remains unclear whether these simulations reflect precise user-specific beliefs or whether they are highly sensitive to semantically independent changes in conversational contexts. In this work, we study counterfactual context revision as a framework for auditing LLM-based stance simulation. Given an original online conversation, we first infer a target user's stance toward a specific topic. We then apply controlled revision strategies to the conversational context and simulate the user's stance again under the revised context. We compare text-only revision strategies with a multimodal one that incorporates meme-based context and evaluate two main effectiveness metrics, i.e., average directional stance shift and stance transition rate. The results reveal effective and robust stance transitions in both text-only and multimodal strategies across different polarization-preference mechanisms. Our study contributes an evaluation framework for understanding the context sensitivity of LLM-based stance simulation. More broadly, it highlights both the promise and risk of using LLMs to simulate online opinion dynamics.

</details>


### [200] [Latent Reasoning with Normalizing Flows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06447)
*Guancheng Tu,Xiangjun Fu,Suhao Yu,Yao Tang,Haoqiang Kang,Lianhui Qin,Yizhe Zhang,Jiatao Gu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: NF-CoT introduces a latent reasoning framework that utilizes normalizing flows to enhance language model reasoning without sacrificing advantages of explicit chain-of-thought methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve reasoning in large language models by overcoming the limitations of textual chain-of-thought approaches.

Method: The NF-CoT framework uses normalizing flows within the LLM backbone to model continuous thoughts while enabling compatibility with existing autoregressive methods.

Result: NF-CoT demonstrates improved pass rates in code generation tasks compared to explicit chain-of-thought methods and previous latent reasoning methods, while reducing reasoning costs.

Conclusion: The proposed NF-CoT framework successfully combines the benefits of latent reasoning and explicit CoT, facilitating efficient generation and optimization of thoughts in language models.

Abstract: Large language models often improve reasoning by generating explicit chain-of-thought (CoT), demonstrating the importance of intermediate computation. However, textual CoT forces this computation through a discrete, serial, and communication-oriented token stream: each reasoning step must be verbalized before the model can proceed, even when the underlying update is semantic, uncertain, or only partially formed. Latent reasoning offers a higher-bandwidth alternative by performing intermediate computation in compact continuous states before committing to text. Yet existing latent-reasoning methods often sacrifice key advantages that make CoT effective in autoregressive language models, including native left-to-right generation, probabilistic sampling, compatibility with KV-cache decoding, and tractable likelihood estimation. We propose NF-CoT, a latent reasoning framework that preserves these advantages by modeling continuous thoughts with normalizing flows. NF-CoT instantiates a TARFlow-style normalizing flow inside the LLM backbone, defining a tractable probability model over compact continuous thoughts distilled from explicit CoT. Continuous-thought positions are generated by an NF head, while text positions are generated by the standard LM head within the same causal stream. This design provides exact likelihoods for latent thoughts, enables probabilistic left-to-right decoding with the original KV cache, and supports direct policy-gradient optimization in the latent reasoning space. On code-generation benchmarks, NF-CoT improves pass rates over explicit-CoT and prior latent-reasoning baselines while substantially reducing intermediate-reasoning cost.

</details>


### [201] [Human Adults and LLMs as Scientists: Who Benefits from Active Exploration?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06464)
*Mandana Samiei,Eunice Yiu,Anthony GX-Chen,Dongyan Lin,Jocelyn Shen,Blake A. Richards,Alison Gopnik,Doina Precup*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The study investigates whether adults' difficulty with conjunctive causal rules persists when they can actively explore causal scenarios. It finds that active exploration enhances performance in identifying these rules, but they still require more testing compared to disjunctive rules. Additionally, human performance is compared to large language models, which show similar gaps in causal reasoning and less effective exploration strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine if the 'conjunctive handicap' in causal reasoning persists when adults have agency through active exploration, as previous findings were limited by passive observation.

Method: Participants engaged in a modified 'blicket detector' task, allowing them to actively explore and identify causal objects under both conjunctive and disjunctive conditions.

Result: Active exploration significantly improved adults' ability in conjunctive causal reasoning, though these rules still required more tests than disjunctive rules. Human performance was also compared to various large language models, revealing similar performance gaps.

Conclusion: The findings suggest that while active exploration aids in understanding conjunctive rules, the inherent difficulty remains, with implications for the efficiency of exploration strategies among both humans and language models.

Abstract: A long-standing finding in the causal learning literature is that adults struggle to identify conjunctive causal rules, where an effect requires the simultaneous presence of multiple causes, while performing better in disjunctive settings. However, most demonstrations of this ``conjunctive handicap'' rely on passive observation paradigms with limited evidence, where learners have no control over evidence generation. This paper asks whether this bias persists when adults are granted agency through active exploration. Using a modified ``blicket detector'' task, adult participants freely intervened to identify causal objects under conjunctive or disjunctive rule structures. We show that active exploration substantially improves adults' conjunctive causal reasoning, although conjunctive rules still require more tests to infer than disjunctive rules. We further compare human performance to a range of large language models in the same setting. While some state-of-the-art models approach human-level performance on hypothesis inference accuracy, they often exhibit less efficient exploration strategies and similar conjunctive-disjunctive performance gaps.

</details>


### [202] [You Only Index Once: Cross-Layer Sparse Attention with Shared Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06467)
*Yutao Sun,Yanqi Zhang,Li Dong,Jianyong Wang,Furu Wei*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Cross-Layer Sparse Attention (CLSA) to enhance the efficiency and quality of long-context inference in large language models (LLMs), achieving significant speed and throughput improvements without sacrificing accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the limitations of existing sparse attention methods that compromise either efficiency or quality during long-context inference in reasoning-heavy tasks.

Method: CLSA utilizes KV-sharing architectures and introduces a routing index that allows token-level top-k selection to be shared across cross-decoder layers, reducing routing overhead while maintaining selectivity.

Result: CLSA achieves up to 7.6x decoding speedup and 17.1x overall throughput improvement on benchmarks for both short and long-context tasks.

Conclusion: CLSA presents an effective architectural solution for enhancing both quality and efficiency in long-context LLMs.

Abstract: Long-context inference in modern LLMs is increasingly constrained by decoding efficiency, especially in reasoning-heavy settings where models generate long intermediate chains of thought. Existing sparse attention methods often face a practical efficiency-quality trade-off. Structured block sparse methods typically provide stronger acceleration but incur noticeable quality loss, while token sparse methods are usually more accurate yet deliver limited end-to-end speedup because top-k routing over the full cache remains expensive. In this work, we propose cross-layer sparse attention (CLSA), which is built on top of KV-sharing architectures such as YOCO. The core idea is to share not only the KV cache across cross-decoder layers, but also the routing index. A single indexer computes token-level top-k selection once and reuses the resulting index across layers, thereby preserving the fine-grained selectivity of token sparse attention while amortizing the routing overhead. The resulting architecture improves all major inference bottlenecks jointly, including pre-filling, KV-cache storage, and long-context decoding. Experiments across short-context and long-context benchmarks show that CLSA is both accurate and efficient, achieving up to 7.6x decoding speedup and 17.1x overall throughput improvement at 128K context. These results suggest a more complete architectural solution for long-context LLMs that jointly advances model quality and inference efficiency.

</details>


### [203] [Self-Augmenting Retrieval for Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06474)
*Paul Jünger,Justin Lovelace,Linxi Zhao,Dongyoung Go,Kilian Q. Weinberger*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SARDI enhances discrete diffusion language models by utilizing low-confidence tokens as lookahead signals for retrieval-augmented generation, improving performance on multi-hop QA tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To leverage the discarded low-confidence tokens in discrete diffusion models for better retrieval and generation outcomes in text tasks.

Method: Introducing Self-Augmenting Retrieval for Diffusion Language Models (SARDI), which utilizes low-confidence tokens to guide the retrieval process during denoising in a training-free and retriever-agnostic manner.

Result: SARDI surpasses current state-of-the-art training-free diffusion and autoregressive retrieval approaches with up to 8 times higher throughput across five multi-hop QA benchmarks.

Conclusion: The approach demonstrates that even low-confidence signals can significantly improve retrieval tasks in text generation, enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of diffusion models.

Abstract: Discrete diffusion language models generate text by iteratively denoising an entire response in parallel. At each step, they predict tentative tokens for every masked position, committing the confident predictions to the output and discarding the unconfident ones. We show that the discarded tokens are in fact a useful lookahead signal for retrieval-augmented generation: even low-confidence tokens often surface salient entities early in the denoising trajectory, enabling retrieval of stronger evidence before the output is finalized. We exploit this through Self-Augmenting Retrieval for Diffusion Language Models (SARDI), a dynamic RAG framework that uses these lookahead tokens to guide retrieval during denoising. SARDI is training-free, retriever-agnostic, and applicable to any reasoning-capable discrete diffusion language model. Across five multi-hop QA benchmarks, SARDI outperforms current training-free diffusion and autoregressive retrieval baselines at up to $8\times$ higher throughput.

</details>


### [204] [Operation-Guided Progressive Human-to-AI Text Transformation Benchmark for Multi-Granularity AI-Text Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06481)
*Sondos Mahmoud Bsharat,Jiacheng Liu,Xiaohan Zhao,Tianjun Yao,Xinyi Shang,Yi Tang,Jiacheng Cui,Ahmed Elhagry,Salwa K. Al Khatib,Hao Li,Salman Khan,Zhiqiang Shen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents OpAI-Bench, a benchmark for studying the influence of human-AI co-editing on document authorship detection across various granularities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how AI authorship signals evolve through the human-AI co-editing process, as current benchmarks focus primarily on final outputs.

Method: OpAI-Bench generates nine revised versions of human-written documents by applying predefined AI coverage levels and five AI edit operations, facilitating evaluation with multiple detection models.

Result: Experiments showed that detectability depends on the proportion of AI edits, the type of edit operation, and the document domain, with mixed-authorship versions often being less detectable than extremes.

Conclusion: OpAI-Bench serves as a valuable tool for analyzing the detectability of AI-assisted writing throughout the revision process in real-world scenarios.

Abstract: As AI writing assistants become increasingly integrated into real-world drafting and revision workflows, many documents are no longer purely human-written or AI-generated, but instead result from progressive human-AI co-editing. However, existing AI-text detection benchmarks largely focus on final outputs and provide limited understanding of how AI authorship signals emerge, accumulate, or disappear throughout the revision process. We introduce OpAI-Bench, an operation-guided benchmark for studying progressive human-to-AI text transformation across document, sentence, token, and span granularities. Starting from human-written documents, OpAI-Bench constructs nine sequentially revised versions for each sample under predefined AI coverage levels and five representative AI edit operations, covering four domains while preserving complete authorship provenance at multiple granularities. The benchmark supports comprehensive evaluation with 8 document-level detectors, 7 sentence-level detectors, and 2 fine-grained token/span-level detectors. Experiments reveal that AI-text detectability is governed not only by the proportion of AI-edited content, but also by edit operation, domain, and cumulative revision history. Interestingly, we notice that mixed-authorship intermediate versions are often harder to detect than both fully human and heavily AI-edited endpoints, exposing non-monotonic detection patterns missed by existing benchmarks. OpAI-Bench provides a controlled testbed for analyzing whether, when, and how AI-assisted writing becomes detectable under realistic progressive editing scenarios. Our code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/VILA-Lab/OpAI-Bench.

</details>


<div id='cs.CR'></div>

# cs.CR [[Back]](#toc)

### [205] [Domain-Conditioned Safety in Frontier Computer-Using Agents: A 793-Episode Browser Benchmark, a Coding-Domain Cross-Reference, and a Reproducibility Audit of Recent Red-Teaming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05233)
*Nicholas Saban*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Study investigates effectiveness of prompt-injection attacks on current CUA models, finding low success rates against advanced agents despite higher reported rates in past studies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate the applicability of previous prompt-injection attack techniques on current state-of-the-art computer-using agents and address discrepancies in attack success rates.

Method: Released CUA-HandCrafted benchmark featuring 793 episodes and 56 attack templates to test against Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.4, measuring multi-step attack success rates.

Result: Achieved 0/140 multi-step attack success rate, indicating resistance to prompt injection, contrasting with higher success rates in prior studies.

Conclusion: High attack success rates in literature are primarily due to RL-optimized strings rather than inherent attack effectiveness, leading to unreproducible ASR without context-sensitive evaluations.

Abstract: Recent computer-using-agent (CUA) red-teaming papers report prompt-injection attack success rates (ASR) of 42-98%, but these headline numbers cluster on retired models and on the most-vulnerable model in each paper's panel. We ask whether those techniques, reproduced as hand-crafted templates, still work against current frontier CUAs. We release CUA-HandCrafted, a public benchmark of 793 episodes spanning 24 multi-step web tasks, 56 attack templates, 8 attack families, and 4 system-prompt configurations. Against Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.4 we measure 0/140 multi-step attack success (Clopper-Pearson 95% upper bound 2.60%); a prompt ablation shows this resistance lives in the model weights. Yet it does not generalize: on a sister coding-agent benchmark (SkillBench), the same weights fall to hand-crafted skill-injection at up to 100%. We argue that the literature's high ASR is largely attributable to RL-optimized injection text rather than the attack categories, and that frontier safety hardening is domain-conditioned, specific to the heavily-targeted browser surface. Reporting techniques without releasing the optimized strings, or extrapolating browser-domain safety to other CUA modalities, makes published ASR numbers unreproducible.

</details>


### [206] [Search-Time Contamination in Deep Research Agents: Measuring Performance Inflation in Public Benchmark Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05241)
*Yongjie Wang,Xinyue Zhang,Kunhong Yao,Zhiwei Zeng,Kaisong Song,Jun Lin,Zhiqi Shen*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper studies Search-Time Contamination (STC) in large language model evaluations, identifying types of leakage in external retrieval that inflate measured performance and advocating for improved evaluation practices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the fragility of public benchmarks for evaluating LLMs due to the retrieval of external data during inference, which can skew results and misrepresent true reasoning abilities.

Method: The authors define three leakage types related to external retrieval and develop detection algorithms to assess their presence and impact on agent performance across multiple benchmarks.

Result: The study finds that STC is prevalent among modern deep research agents, leading to performance inflation of up to 4% on evaluated benchmarks.

Conclusion: The conclusion highlights the need for contamination-aware practices in evaluating LLMs to ensure accurate assessments of reasoning capabilities.

Abstract: Public benchmarks enable fair and reproducible evaluation of LLM reasoning, but they become fragile for deep research agents that actively search the web during inference. Such agents may retrieve public benchmark metadata, question context, or even ground-truth answers via web search. This gives rise to Search-Time Contamination (STC), where external retrieval bypasses intended reasoning and inflates measured performance. We systematically study STC in deep research agent evaluation. We define three contamination types with increasing severity, namely Benchmark Metadata Leakage, Question-Context Leakage, and Explicit Answer Leakage, and develop detection algorithms to identify them and quantify their impact on agent performance. Evaluating modern deep research agents on six public benchmarks, we find that STC is widespread and can inflate performance by up to 4%. Our findings show that existing evaluations may overestimate true reasoning ability. We therefore advocate contamination-aware practices, including isolated sandboxes, transparent search trajectories, and controlled benchmark access.

</details>


### [207] [From Attack Simulation to SIEM Rule: Deterministic Detection-as-Code Synthesis with Probe-Level Traceability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05252)
*Alexandre Cristovão Maiorano*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper discusses a method for automating the translation of attack simulation findings into Sigma detection rules, aiming to improve the efficiency of security monitoring systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To streamline the process of creating detection rules from simulation findings, reducing manual effort and enhancing SIEM integration.

Method: The authors present a deterministic synthesis function that maps BAS findings to Sigma rules using a template library categorized by OWASP and MITRE ATT&CK.

Result: The method successfully generates starter rules from every probe finding in locked corpora, with rules compatible with Splunk and Elasticsearch. Testing shows practical effectiveness of rules with a manageable false positive rate.

Conclusion: The approach offers a reliable method for deriving detection rules directly from attack simulations, enabling reproducibility and a clear traceable relationship between alerts and probing origins.

Abstract: Security teams routinely simulate attacks against their own systems to check whether their monitoring would catch a real intruder. These Breach-and-Attack-Simulation (BAS) tools surface findings, but the security information and event management (SIEM) systems that watch production need detection rules -- and today a human bridges that gap by hand, reading each finding and writing the corresponding Sigma rule (a vendor-neutral detection format). We show this translation can be partially automated when probes are drawn from a locked corpus, so each finding carries a stable identifier back to the originating probe. We describe a deterministic synthesis function that maps each finding to a starter Sigma rule through a small template library (N=23, indexed by categories from the OWASP LLM and Web Top 10), with a back-reference to the originating finding and its MITRE ATT&CK technique. On two locked corpora (17-probe LLM, 23-probe Web), every bypassed-probe finding yields a starter rule, and all 17/17 emitted rules parse and convert to Splunk and Elasticsearch backends. Replayed through a live OpenSearch SIEM, the LLM rules fire on 30% of a held-out AdvBench subset and 14% of HarmBench at 7.7% false positives on a benign baseline; the Web side is validated structurally, not against a held-out attack set. The contribution is a verifiable, byte-stable path from BAS finding to operator-deployable starter rule, re-derivable from the published corpus and template library alone -- trading the breadth of LLM-generative methods for exact reproducibility and a typed traceback from any fired alert to the originating probe.

</details>


### [208] [Willing but Unable: Separating Refusal from Capability in Code LLMs via Abliteration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05396)
*Cristina Carleo,Pietro Liguori,Naghmeh Ivaki,Domenico Cotroneo*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper investigates abliteration, a method to enable language models to inject specified vulnerabilities into safe code by overcoming refusal issues from LLMs, specifically exploring its impact on code generation across different model sizes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The study addresses challenges in generating labeled vulnerable code for learning-based vulnerability detection due to label noise and LLMs' systematic refusal to execute injection prompts for vulnerabilities.

Method: The method involves a low-rank weight edit called abliteration to modify the LLM's response patterns, using Python and CWE-89 (SQL injection) as a case study, testing models with 3B, 7B, and 14B parameters on different safe code samples.

Result: Abliteration successfully reduced refusal rates to zero or near-zero, while maintaining a high level of syntactic validity (above 93%), revealing a disconnect between the model's response willingness and generation capability.

Conclusion: The findings suggest that abliteration effectively enables LLMs to perform vulnerability injection, while emphasizing that the capacity for such actions is dependent on model size.

Abstract: Producing a labeled vulnerable code at scale is a recurring obstacle for learning-based vulnerability detection: mined corpora carry substantial label noise, and existing LLM-based augmentation propagates these inaccuracies because it transforms vulnerable seeds rather than synthesising vulnerabilities from a specification. A complementary route is to start from safe code and ask an instruction-tuned LLM to inject a specified CWE (which would shift the labeling burden from open-ended detection to bounded binary confirmation) but safety-aligned code LLMs systematically refuse such prompts. This paper is a preliminary feasibility study of abliteration, a low-rank weight edit that orthogonally projects out the refusal direction in the residual stream, as a tool to remove this barrier. We use Python and CWE-89 (SQL injection) as a case study, evaluating the Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct family at 3B, 7B, and 14B parameters on safe samples drawn from PromSec and SafeCoder, replicated three times per condition. We find that (i) refusal on injection prompts is strongly size- and prompt-context-dependent: the 14B refuses 100% of prompts, the 7B refuses 73% of PromSec but only 5% of SafeCoder, whereas the 3B is essentially never blocked; (ii) abliteration reduces refusal to zero or near-zero across all sizes while leaving syntactic validity above 93%, supporting the view that, in this setting, refusal can be detached from measured code-generation capability; and (iii) the post-abliteration injection rate remains capacity-bound (88-97% on the 14B, 89-90% on the 7B, and 25-48% on the 3B) separating willingness, which abliteration unlocks, from capability, which scales with parameters. Vulnerability verdicts are produced by a three-tool detector ensemble (CodeQL, Semgrep, Bandit) followed by manual adjudication by two authors on detector-positive outputs.

</details>


### [209] [A formal framework for the economic security of DeFi compositions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05418)
*Massimo Bartoletti,Riccado Marchesin,Roberto Zunino*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper introduces a formal security notion, MEV non-interference, to address the security risks associated with the composability of Decentralized Finance (DeFi) services. It provides a framework to analyze and ensure economic security in DeFi smart contract interactions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper seeks to address the security vulnerabilities arising from the composability of DeFi services, where interactions between new and existing smart contracts can be exploited by adversaries.

Method: The authors define MEV non-interference and local MEV, proposing a modular reasoning framework that distinguishes secure from vulnerable DeFi compositions, using two adversarial models based on wealth.

Result: The framework enables the analysis of various DeFi compositions, providing sufficient conditions for secure composability and identifying vulnerable contracts in several applications like exchanges and lending pools.

Conclusion: The findings contribute to a formal understanding of the economic security of DeFi, guiding the design of more secure smart contract interactions.

Abstract: Decentralized Finance (DeFi) services are usually constructed by composing a variety of smart contracts. While composability is a key driver of the success of DeFi, it also creates security risks: adversaries may exploit interactions between newly deployed contracts and the pre-existing ones to inflict economic losses. We introduce MEV non-interference, a formal security notion for DeFi composability requiring that the maximal extractable value from a set of newly deployed contracts is not increased by interactions with the existing blockchain state. To support this notion, we define local MEV, a novel measure of economic attacks that focusses on the loss of a given set of victim contracts. We study two adversarial models, with bounded and unbounded wealth, and establish sufficient conditions and locality principles that enable modular reasoning about secure composability. We apply the framework to representative DeFi compositions, including exchanges, AMMs, options, lending pools, routers, and arbitrage contracts, showing how it distinguishes secure compositions from vulnerable ones. Our results provide a formal foundation for reasoning about the economic security of DeFi compositions.

</details>


### [210] [SHIELDS: Automating OS Hardening with Iterative Multi-Agent Remediation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05476)
*Andrew Hamara,Dwight Horne,Aldehir Rojas,Timothy Kurniawan,Sophie Lamothe,Vishal Suresh,Nicholas Turoci,Lawrence Wong*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: SHIELDS is a multi-agent system using large language models to automate OS hardening by proposing and refining security fixes based on system feedback, achieving 73% remediation of compliance issues, independent of model size.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of security misconfigurations leading to OS-level compromises and the inefficiency of manual compliance processes with standards like DISA STIGs.

Method: SHIELDS employs large language models in a multi-agent framework to iteratively propose and refine remediation actions based on ongoing feedback from system execution and validation scans.

Result: The evaluation demonstrated that SHIELDS can successfully remediate up to 73% of identified scan issues across various virtual machine configurations, with effectiveness influenced more by tool utilization than model size.

Conclusion: The findings indicate a viable approach for automating security compliance that is adaptable to environments with limited computing resources or stringent privacy requirements.

Abstract: Security misconfigurations remain a leading cause of OS-level compromise, and manually keeping systems compliant with standards like Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guides (STIGs) is a tedious and expensive process. Existing compliance automation tools can reduce some of this burden, but they depend on static, pre-written corrective actions. In this paper, we introduce SHIELDS, a multi-agent system that uses large language models (LLMs) to approach OS hardening as an iterative, feedback-driven process. Instead of applying fixed remediations, SHIELDS continuously proposes fixes and refines them based on feedback from target system execution and validation scans. We evaluate the system across multiple virtual machine configurations using six contemporary LLMs ranging from 20B to 400B parameters, and find that SHIELDS successfully remediates up to 73% of scan findings. Our results also suggest that success in this setting depends less on model size (parameter count) than on effective tool use and information gathering, paving a practical path toward reducing the burden of security compliance in environments where compute is limited or security and privacy needs drive local model use.

</details>


### [211] [Policy-Compliant Cloud Storage Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05423)
*Dimitrios Stavrakakis,Masanori Misono,Julian Pritzi,Harshavardhan Unnibhavi,Nuno Santos,Pramod Bhatotia*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: GDPRuler is a middleware system that ensures GDPR compliance for key-value stores (KVS) on untrusted clouds without modifying their code, maintaining low performance overheads.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the challenges of GDPR compliance in KVS, particularly in untrusted cloud environments, where existing solutions require invasive modifications or introduce performance issues.

Method: GDPRuler operates as a trusted middleware, utilizing a Confidential Virtual Machine (CVM) to enforce compliance, manage metadata, and log audits while employing a declarative policy language to translate GDPR obligations into rules.

Result: GDPRuler shows low performance overheads, achieving ~61% throughput of native KVS and minimal metadata storage costs while enhancing query speeds significantly (13-182x) through efficient indexing.

Conclusion: By implementing GDPR compliance via a traceable and efficient middleware, GDPRuler presents a viable solution for maintaining lawful data management in KVS deployed on untrusted clouds.

Abstract: Privacy regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) impose strict requirements on how personal data is stored, processed, and audited. While key-value stores (KVS) are widely used in latency-sensitive applications, their simple data model and untrusted cloud deployment environments make GDPR compliance particularly challenging. Existing approaches require invasive code modifications, impose high performance overheads, or overlook the integrity of compliance mechanisms themselves.
  This paper presents GDPRuler, a trusted middleware system that enables verifiable GDPR compliance for KVS on untrusted clouds without modifying their codebase. GDPRuler deploys a trusted GDPR monitor inside a Confidential Virtual Machine (CVM), which enforces GDPR policies, manages compliance metadata, and maintains tamper-evident audit logs. A declarative policy language translates core GDPR obligations into enforceable runtime rules. To ensure efficiency, GDPRuler encodes metadata compactly within KV records, builds dedicated metadata indexes for GDPR-specific queries, and logs only compliance-relevant events in a space-efficient format. We implement GDPRuler as a transparent proxy for unmodified Redis and RocksDB deployments. Evaluation with YCSB and GDPR-inspired workloads shows that GDPRuler enforces core compliance guarantees with low overheads: GDPRuler achieves ~61% of native KVS throughput with the CVM environment contributing 28%-32% of it, metadata storage overhead remains below 20%, and GDPR queries benefit from 13-182x speedup through metadata indexing. By embedding verifiable policy enforcement into a trusted middleware layer, GDPRuler offers a practical path toward GDPR-compliant KVS on untrusted cloud infrastructures.

</details>


### [212] [ZERO-APT: A Closed-Loop Adversarial Framework for LLM-Driven Automated Penetration Testing under Intelligent Defense](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05567)
*Anlan Zheng,Tiantian Zhu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: ZERO-APT is a framework for evaluating LLM-driven penetration testing agents against intelligent defense, addressing realism, consistency, and auditability by integrating a LLM Defender, separating planning and execution, and introducing an adjudicator.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve the evaluation of LLM-driven penetration testing agents by accounting for realistic defense scenarios and enhancing traceability of their actions.
