TL;DR: The paper introduces the Recuse Signal, a cooperative access control mechanism for LLM agents, allowing them to voluntarily withdraw from restricted resources, demonstrating its effectiveness in a controlled experiment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM agents operate autonomously and hold valid credentials, there's a need for a mechanism to communicate off-limit resources without compromising security.

Method: The paper proposes a Recuse Signal, implements it via SSH and PostgreSQL adapters, and conducts an experiment monitoring agent compliance during benign tasks.

Result: In the pilot experiment, agents demonstrated 100% compliance by recusing themselves when the Recuse Signal was present, contrasting with 100% task completion without the signal.

Conclusion: The Recuse Signal behaves as a cooperative governance tool; its implementation fosters compliance among LLM agents, with implications for operator control in autonomous systems.

Abstract: As autonomous LLM agents increasingly hold real credentials and operate infrastructure without a human in the loop, operators have no standard way to tell an agent that a resource is off-limits. Access controls either let the agent in (it has valid credentials) or hard-fail it (indistinguishable from any other client). We propose a third mode: a lightweight, published in-band deny signal -- the Recuse Signal -- that a server emits over a protocol's existing channels (an SSH banner, a PostgreSQL NOTICE) asking a connecting automated agent to voluntarily withdraw. This is a cooperative governance control, the robots.txt analogue for live access; it is explicitly not a security boundary. Its value is entirely empirical and, to our knowledge, unmeasured: do compliant LLM agents actually honor such a signal? We define the signal as an open mini-standard, implement two zero- or low-footprint adapters (an SSH banner/PAM hook and a PostgreSQL wire-protocol proxy), deploy them on a live production host, and run a controlled experiment in which fresh agents are given a benign operations task and observed for recusal. In a pilot (SSH; OpenAI GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini; and Claude Code as a deployed agent), the signal cleanly induces recusal -- 100% recusal when present versus 100% task completion in a no-signal control -- and, revealingly, behaves as a cooperative rather than absolute signal: an explicit operator-authorization framing flips the most capable model to proceed, while other agents continue to defer to the on-host policy. We release the standard, adapters, and experiment harness for reproduction.

</details>


<div id='cs.DB'></div>

# cs.DB [[Back]](#toc)

### [243] [QDAG: Declarative Composition of Reusable Analytics Methodologies at LinkedIn](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05662)
*Peter Ho,Praveen Chaganlal,Tianle Zhang,Endong Zhu*

Main category: cs.DB

TL;DR: QDAG is a production system that represents analytics methodologies as declarative directed acyclic graphs to improve efficiency and consistency in data analytics at LinkedIn.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses issues of repeated orchestration code, definition drift, and testing challenges in reusable analytics methodologies.

Method: QDAG models analytics methodologies as a declarative directed acyclic graph (DAG) composed of typed steps, executing various operations like queries and transformations.

Result: QDAG has been deployed on over 500 hosts for more than 100 use cases, introducing minimal orchestration delays and maintaining low latency.

Conclusion: Deciding on a declarative design for methodologies enhances their reusability, testability, and consistency across products without sacrificing performance.

Abstract: Production analytics products often depend on reusable methodologies: multi-step definitions such as headcount growth, top-skill growth, or differentially-private impression distributions. Although these methodologies define business-critical numbers, they are commonly implemented as imperative glue around OLAP queries, service calls, joins, transformations, and conditional logic. As a result, teams duplicate orchestration code, definitions drift across products, and methodologies are difficult to test or analyze.
  We present QDAG, a production system at LinkedIn that represents an analytics methodology as a declarative directed acyclic graph of typed steps. Nodes may execute Apache Pinot queries, downstream service calls, in-memory SQLite joins, jq transformations, conditionals, differentially-private aggregations, or calls to other QDAGs. The engine evaluates graphs demand-driven, memoized, pruned, and parallelized in the per-request analytics mid-tier. QDAG is deployed across more than 500 hosts and over 100 production use cases, adding roughly 10 ms median orchestration overhead and under 50 ms at the 99th percentile. Our experience shows that making methodologies declarative improves reuse, testability, and cross-product consistency while preserving interactive latency.

</details>


### [244] [Data Flow Control: Data Safety Policies for AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05679)
*Charlie Summers,Eugene Wu*

Main category: cs.DB

TL;DR: The paper presents Data Flow Control (DFC), a framework for enforcing data safety policies in SQL queries that ensure regulatory and privacy compliance without incurring performance overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the issue that while SQL queries can be syntactically correct, they may still violate crucial regulatory and business constraints, highlighting the need for an enforced safety mechanism in data infrastructure.

Method: Data Flow Control (DFC) is introduced as a framework that allows for declarative specification of data safety policies, with a novel query rewriting layer, Passant, which operates without the need for materializing provenance data.

Result: Passant shows approximately 0% overhead during execution across various DBMS engines, significantly outperforming existing alternatives in terms of efficiency and scalability.

Conclusion: Data Flow Control lays the groundwork for integrating data safety into data infrastructure, moving away from reliance on user prompts and retrospective checks.

Abstract: Agents increasingly generate SQL, orchestrate pipelines, and automate data analysis on behalf of users. While recent work improves query correctness, correctness is not safety. A query may be semantically valid yet violate regulatory, privacy, or business constraints that govern how data may be combined and released. We argue that enforcing such constraints is fundamentally a data infrastructure problem.
  This paper introduces Data Flow Control (DFC), a framework to declaratively specify and guarantee policy enforcement over tuple-level data flows within a DBMS query. A key challenge is defining a policy language that is optimizer-invariant yet efficient to enforce at scale. We formalize data safety as aggregate predicates over provenance monomials and present Passant, a portable query rewriting layer that enforces DFC policies without materializing provenance. Across five DBMS engines -- DuckDB, Umbra, PostgreSQL, DataFusion, and SQLServer -- Passant achieves ~0% overhead and outperforms alternatives by orders of magnitude. As a result, Data Flow Control is the first step towards moving data safety from prompts and post-hoc checks into the data infrastructure. Data Flow Control is available open source at https://github.com/dataflowcontrol/data-flow-control.

</details>


### [245] [Causal Scaffolding for Physical Reasoning: A Benchmark for Causally-Informed Physical World Understanding in VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05966)
*Tianyi Tang,Zhuoyi Lin,Zeyu Feng,Tianyi Ma,Yew-Soon Ong,Ivor Tsang,Haiyan Yin*

Main category: cs.DB

TL;DR: CausalPhys introduces a benchmark for evaluating vision-language models' (VLMs) causal reasoning capabilities, revealing systematic weaknesses and proposing a new fine-tuning method for improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the inadequacy of current VLMs in causal physical reasoning, as they often provide plausible but incorrect answers, highlighting a gap in their understanding of the physical world.

Method: CausalPhys comprises over 3,000 annotated questions with causal graphs outlining object-attribute-event dependencies and introduces a causal-graph-grounded metric for evaluating VLM reasoning accuracy.

Result: Analysis using the new metric shows that leading VLMs have significant deficiencies in causal reasoning, indicating the need for enhanced learning methods.

Conclusion: The introduction of Causal Rationale-informed Fine-Tuning (CRFT) bolsters reasoning accuracy and interpretability, setting a robust groundwork for future advancements in causally aware VLMs.

Abstract: Understanding and reasoning about the physical world is the foundation of intelligent behavior, yet state-of-the-art vision-language models (VLMs) still fail at causal physical reasoning, often producing plausible but incorrect answers. To address this gap, we introduce CausalPhys, a benchmark of over 3,000 carefully curated video- and image-based questions spanning four domains: Perception, Anticipation, Intervention, and Goal Orientation. Each question is paired with an expert-annotated causal graph capturing object-attribute-event dependencies, enabling interpretable and fine-grained evaluation of causal understanding. Building on this, we formulate a causal-graph-grounded metric that quantitatively measures how well a model's chain-of-thought reasoning aligns with the correct causal relations, moving beyond answer-only accuracy and enabling systematic diagnosis of VLMs' causal reasoning failures. Using this metric, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of leading VLMs, revealing systematic gaps in capturing causal dependencies and underscoring the need for causality-aware learning. To address these limitations, we further propose Causal Rationale-informed Fine-Tuning (CRFT), which explicitly aligns VLM reasoning with causal structures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CRFT substantially enhances both reasoning accuracy and interpretability across multiple model backbones. By unifying dataset curation, causal evaluation, and causality-informed learning, CausalPhys establishes a strong foundation for advancing modern VLMs toward causally grounded physical reasoning.

</details>


### [246] [Validation of graph databases against PG-Schema](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06127)
*Jacek Ciszewski,Jakub Kłos,Maxime Jakubowski,Dominik Tomaszuk,Filip Murlak*

Main category: cs.DB

TL;DR: Validating a graph database against a PG-Schema is NP-complete in combined complexity but PTIME in data complexity; restrictions on type combinations improve efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To classify the complexity of graph database validation against PG-Schema graphs.

Method: Analyzing NP-completeness and data complexity through the lens of graph validation without integrity constraints.

Result: The problem is NP-complete in combined complexity but can be solved in PTIME for data complexity when restricted appropriately.

Conclusion: With the right restrictions on type combinations and unions, the validation problem can be efficiently solved in PTIME.

Abstract: The problem of validating a given graph database instance against a given PG-Schema graph type without integrity constraints is NP- complete in terms of combined complexity and in PTIME in terms of data complexity. The combined complexity drops to PTIME when the alternation between type combinations and unions is suitably restricted

</details>


### [247] [TOKI: A Bitemporal Operator Algebra for Contradiction Resolution in LLM-Agent Persistent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06240)
*Ziming Wang*

Main category: cs.DB

TL;DR: The paper introduces TOKI, a framework for ensuring write-time correctness in LLM agents' belief updates, addressing anomalies in existing production systems' resolution heuristics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing resolution heuristics in LLM agents lack clarity in their isolation levels and anomalies, necessitating a formal contract for write-time concurrency control.

Method: The TOKI framework classifies existing heuristics as bitemporal operators with explicit isolation preconditions and provenance annotations, proving soundness through four theorems and extending guarantees to operator pipelines.

Result: TOKI eliminates three common write-time anomalies while maintaining a language-model judge, proving more reliable than other systems that compromise on this aspect.

Conclusion: The contribution of this paper is a formalized connection between write-time correctness and resolution heuristics, providing a clear specification for production systems that has not been previously established.

Abstract: Persistent memory for an LLM agent is a write-heavy substrate: every belief update is a versioned write, and a new claim may contradict a stored one. Production systems use four resolution heuristics (last-writer-wins, evidence-weighted merge, await-confirmation, per-rule policy), yet none declares the isolation level it assumes or the write-time anomalies it admits. We show that contradiction resolution is write-time concurrency control and make the missing contract explicit. TOKI types the four heuristics as one family of bitemporal operators over a dual-row schema, each with an isolation precondition and a provenance annotation that preserves the losing fact in an audit row. Four soundness theorems close the contract across isolation, schema, and provenance, lift the guarantees to operator pipelines, and extend the fold operators to n-ary conflict sets. A tightness companion proves that, within the relational schedule model, keyed logging of the adjudicating judge is necessary for replay consistency, which every audited baseline omits. A verdict matrix over eight systems localizes the gap: every baseline that keeps a language-model judge on the write path admits at least one of three write-time anomalies (replay inconsistency, belief-drift skew, audit erasure); a content-addressed engine-layer comparator avoids them only by removing the judge, and TOKI alone excludes all three while keeping it. On its one natural-workload slice the audit-row defence moves LoCoMo by 0.86, and ablating the typed memory layer removes 0.49 accuracy on 1,444 answerable LoCoMo questions; the cross-system comparison stays underpowered and claims no superiority. The contribution is the contract: a write-time correctness specification, proved sound across isolation, schema, and provenance, pinning the guarantee every production heuristic assumes but no deployed system makes explicit.

</details>


<div id='cs.NE'></div>

# cs.NE [[Back]](#toc)

### [248] [Quantifying Uncertainty In Wide Two-Layer Neural Networks: On The Law Of The Limiting Fluctuation Process](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05982)
*Arnaud Descours,Arnaud Guillin,Geoffrey Lacour,Manon Michel,Boris Nectoux,Paul Stos*

Main category: cs.NE

TL;DR: The paper presents a method for uncertainty quantification in neural networks predictions by evaluating uncertainty using PDEs, reducing computational costs compared to traditional methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Uncertainty quantification in neural networks is essential for many applications, and existing methods like deep ensembles can be computationally expensive.

Method: The authors analyze the asymptotic variance of wide two-layer neural networks trained with stochastic gradient descent, using a trajectorial central limit theorem to characterize the law of random fluctuations around the mean limit. They derive a covariance representation for this process.

Result: The law of the limiting process is identified as a centered Gaussian process in a weighted Sobolev space. A closed covariance representation for finite-dimensional distributions is also derived.

Conclusion: The derived limiting variance of network-output fluctuations provides insights into uncertainty quantification, illustrated in a one-dimensional regression example.

Abstract: Uncertainty quantification in neural networks prediction is a main issue for usual applications. Our approach seeks at reducing computation costs by directly evaluating uncertainty using PDE's information on the asymptotic variance, rather than the deep ensemble method which may be seen as a Monte Carlo estimation of the prediction, requiring the training of multiple networks. We thus study the law of the limiting process describing the random fluctuations around the mean-field limit of wide two-layer neural networks trained by stochastic gradient descent in a weak-noise regime. Building on a recent trajectorial central limit theorem, in which this limit is characterized as the weak solution of a linear stochastic evolution equation, we identify its law explicitly. More precisely, we show that it is a centered Gaussian process in the dual of a weighted Sobolev space, and we derive a closed covariance representation for the finite-dimensional distributions obtained by testing it against smooth functions. This covariance is expressed through the solution of a backward transport equation with a nonlocal source term, whose coefficients are driven by the mean-field trajectory. As a consequence, by testing against the activation function at a fixed input, we obtain an expression for the limiting variance of the corresponding network-output fluctuations. We illustrate this result numerically on a one-dimensional regression example.

</details>


### [249] [Hub-Aware Hybrid Search: Accelerating the Locally Aligned Ant Technique](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06198)
*Simone Vilardi,Reynier Peletier,Felipe Contreras,Kerstin Bunte*

Main category: cs.NE

TL;DR: This paper proposes a two-stage solution to improve the efficiency of the Locally Aligned Ant Technique (LAAT) in detecting structures in high-dimensional point clouds, particularly in astronomical data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to enhance the detection of multidimensional structures such as filaments and clusters in noisy astronomical data while minimizing computational overhead.

Method: The method involves a two-stage approach: first, identifying and replacing dense hubs with a tailored likelihood model, then applying a mixed likelihood-pheromone strategy to guide ants in navigating these regions.

Result: The proposed solution showed improvements in the detection efficiency and robustness of the LAAT through synthetic tests and a large-scale N-body simulation of the cosmic web.

Conclusion: The findings suggest that the two-stage preprocessing enhances the effectiveness of LAAT in complex high-dimensional scenarios.

Abstract: Finding manifold structures in noisy and high-dimensional point clouds is a challenging but important problem. In astronomical observation survey and simulation data the detection of filaments, streams (1D), walls (2D) and clusters (3D) gives rise to deeper understanding of the evolution of our universe. The Locally Aligned Ant Technique (LAAT) uses biologically inspired agents to efficiently recover faint and multidimensional structures. However, very dense hubs (e.g. nodes or globular clusters) dominate the ants' activity, creating unnecessary computational overheads. In this paper we propose a two-stage solution. First a fast preprocessing step locates the hubs and replaces them with a tailored likelihood model. Subsequently, a mixed likelihood-pheromone strategy guides the ants to efficiently bridge the dense regions. We demonstrate improvements in detection efficiency and robustness of LAAT with synthetic and a large-scale astronomical N-body simulation of the cosmic web.

</details>


<div id='cs.SE'></div>

# cs.SE [[Back]](#toc)

### [250] [Where Do Large Language Models Fail on Competitive Programming? A Taxonomy of Failures by Algorithm Type and Difficulty Rating](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05228)
*Ayush Kumar Jha,Shalini Jha*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This study analyzes the performance of two large language models, GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 4.6, on competitive programming tasks, revealing significant gaps in algorithmic reasoning despite high-level pass rates. It identifies critical failure patterns and assesses the impact of reasoning frameworks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To identify and understand the domain-specific vulnerabilities of LLMs in competitive programming, moving beyond aggregate performance metrics.

Method: A systematic empirical study involving 315 Codeforces problems categorized by algorithm types and difficulty, evaluating the models under controlled conditions with a focus on reasoning frameworks using direct generation and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) techniques.

Result: The study found that forcing CoT reduces GPT-4o's pass rate from 46.0% to 36.8% and significantly increases Compile Errors for Claude, while both models predominantly fail due to wrong answers (WA) in over 90% and 70% of cases, respectively.

Conclusion: Standard prompt engineering does not effectively address the challenges of algorithmic reasoning in competitive programming, highlighting the need for improved models or techniques.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate increasing proficiency on competitive programming benchmarks, yet technical reports predominantly publish aggregate pass rates, obscuring domain-specific vulnerabilities. We present a systematic empirical study of LLM failure patterns using a balanced taxonomy of 315 Codeforces problems across seven algorithm categories and three difficulty tiers. We evaluate GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 4.6 under strict execution-based conditions, controlling for temperature (T = 0.2). To isolate the impact of reasoning frameworks on algorithmic correctness, we conduct an ablation study comparing direct zero-shot generation against zero-shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT). Our findings reveal a severe divergence from standard NLP benchmarks: forcing CoT aggressively penalizes GPT-4o, dropping its pass rate from 46.0% to 36.8% and exacerbating a critical weakness in Greedy logic. Conversely, while Claude maintains a higher logical baseline (63.5% under CoT), the expanded text generation severely degrades its markdown instruction adherence, causing its Compile Errors to more than triple (from 9 to 31, a 244% increase). Furthermore, failure-mode analysis indicates that Wrong Answer (WA) is the dominant verdict for both models--accounting for over 90% of GPT-4o's and roughly 70% of Claude's unaccepted solutions. These findings empirically demonstrate that standard prompt engineering techniques fail to bridge the algorithmic reasoning gap in competitive programming environments.

</details>


### [251] [DeployBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Research Artifact Deployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05238)
*Yuanli Wang,Yaoyao Qian,Yue Zhang,Hanhan Zhou,Jindan Huang,Tianfu Fu,Qiuyang Mang,Huanzhi Mao,Wenhao Chai,Wendong Fan,Liqiang Jing*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: DeployBench is introduced as a multi-domain benchmark comprising 51 research-artifact deployment tasks addressing the challenges in software engineering and machine learning research. It highlights deficiencies in current LLM agents by revealing low pass rates due to failures in task adherence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the difficulties in setting up research artifacts in varied environments, which often hinder reproducibility and usability in software engineering and ML research.

Method: The authors present DeployBench, a benchmark with 51 tasks that test deployment processes across multiple domains, incorporating system dependencies and legacy compatibility, validated through a hidden execution pipeline.

Result: Testing four leading LLMs showed pass rates between 7.8% and 51.0%, with failures primarily due to incorrect task validation checks by agents.

Conclusion: DeployBench underscores the limitations of current LLM agents in autonomous deployment, providing a realistic framework for evaluating and improving performance in scientific research.

Abstract: LLM agents have made rapid progress on software engineering and ML research tasks, but these advances often assume access to a working runnable environment. For research artifacts released alongside published papers, setting up such an environment from a fresh machine remains a major bottleneck. Existing environment setup benchmarks do not cover the full scope of research artifact deployment, which involves multi-language toolchains, system-level dependencies beyond containers (e.g. GPU/CUDA and kernel configurations), and legacy artifact compatibility. We introduce DeployBench, a multi-domain benchmark of 51 research-artifact deployment tasks spanning AI/ML, computer systems, and scientific computing, covering all these dimensions. Each task is verified by a hidden pipeline that executes the paper's designated experiment and checks its outputs. Evaluating four state-of-the-art LLMs with OpenHands yields pass-rates from 7.8% - 51.0% . Failures are dominated by a completion-judgment problem: 97 of 154 are agent-terminated self-stops, where the agent's pre-finish checks validate a different or weaker target than the paper-specific task requires. DeployBench highlights the gap between current agents and autonomous deployment, and offers a realistic testbed for scientific research agents.

</details>


### [252] [SWE-InfraBench: Evaluating Language Models on Cloud Infrastructure Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05249)
*Natalia Tarasova,Enrique Balp-Straffon,Aleksei Iancheruk,Yevhenii Sielskyi,Nikita Kozodoi,Liam H. Byrne,Jack Butler,Dayuan Jiang,Marcin Czelej,Andrew Ang,Yash Shah,Roi Blanco,Sergei Ivanov*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: SWE-InfraBench is a benchmark designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) tasks using AWS CDK, revealing limitations in current LLMs' capabilities for realistic code modifications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explore LLM performance in Infrastructure-as-Code development, particularly for incremental edits in imperative frameworks like AWS CDK, as opposed to declarative benchmarks.

Method: SWE-InfraBench presents a dataset created from multiple real-world IaC codebases, focusing on modifications based on natural language instructions, with evaluation based on passing specific test cases.

Result: Current state-of-the-art LLMs, including Sonnet 3.7 and specialized models like DeepSeek R1, show limited success in these tasks, achieving only 34% and 24% respectively.

Conclusion: The evaluation highlights significant gaps in LLM abilities for IaC, indicating a need for further development to enhance support for complex code modifications in cloud environments.

Abstract: Building infrastructure-as-code (IaC) in cloud computing is a critical task, underpinning the reliability, scalability, and security of modern software systems. Despite the remarkable progress of large language models (LLMs) in software engineering -- demonstrated across many dedicated benchmarks -- their capabilities in developing IaC remain underexplored. Unlike existing IaC benchmarks that predominantly center on declarative paradigms such as Terraform and involve generating entire codebases from scratch, our benchmark reflects the incremental code edits common in enterprise development with imperative tools like the AWS CDK. We present SWE-InfraBench, a diverse evaluation dataset sourced from dozens of real-world IaC codebases that challenge LLMs to perform realistic code modifications in AWS CDK repositories. Each example requires models to implement changes to existing codebases based on natural language instructions, with success determined by passing provided test cases. These tasks demand sophisticated reasoning about cloud resource dependencies and implementation patterns beyond conventional code generation challenges. Our evaluation results reveal significant limitations in current LLMs showing that even state-of-the-art systems struggle with many tasks -- the best model, Sonnet 3.7, succeeds in only 34\% of cases, while specialized reasoning models like DeepSeek R1 achieve just 24% success. The SWE-InfraBench dataset is available at: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/64e59070fd51c0278560b01eb5dc4f3c447d5268cdabe5a350d2969e4413fea5

</details>


### [253] [Towards Persistent Case-Based Memory for Autonomous Data Science: A CBR-Augmented R&D-Agent with a Locally Deployable Small Language Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05250)
*Felix Stocker*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper explores the integration of a Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) layer into an autonomous data-science agent framework, demonstrating improved performance and knowledge transfer through structured data and executable code in comparison to a baseline model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the lack of persistent memory in autonomous data-science agents and improve the effectiveness of data management and knowledge transfer.

Method: The paper integrates a CBR layer into Microsoft's R&D-Agent, leveraging structured case records and a custom backend for Gemma 4. This setup involves a five-gate quality filter and a heuristic reuse-detection mechanism for evaluating knowledge transfer.

Result: The CBR enhancement shows better accuracy on the Kaggle competition Spaceship Titanic (0.8147) compared to the baseline (0.8098) with lower variance, indicating improved performance with the CBR system.

Conclusion: Utilizing CBR for autonomous agents enhances performance and maintains semantic relevance in knowledge transfer, positioning it as a valuable augmentation for data-science applications.

Abstract: Most top-performing autonomous data-science agents rely on frontier cloud models and lack persistent, cross-session memory. This paper addresses two open gaps: (1) the underexplored use of formally structured, quality-controlled Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) case bases coupling symbolic case records with executable code artefacts; and (2) the untested viability of Small Language Models (SLMs) as locally deployable agent backbones. We present CBR-augmented R&D-Agent, integrating a persistent CBR layer into Microsoft's R&D-Agent framework with a custom backend for Gemma 4 31B Dense -- the first published end-to-end evaluation of Gemma 4 as an autonomous data-science agent backbone. The CBR layer overrides three R&D loop phases via a surgical subclass toggled by a single environment variable. Cases are stored as structured records with executable code snapshots and quality metadata; a five-gate quality filter and a heuristic reuse-detection mechanism assess knowledge transfer by combining embedding similarity, code-fingerprint overlap, and injection provenance. Evaluated on two Kaggle competitions (NOMAD 2018, Spaceship Titanic) with four seeds over eight improvement loops each, CBR achieves directionally higher accuracy than the CBR-disabled baseline on Spaceship Titanic (0.8147 vs. 0.8098, d = -1.41) with substantially lower variance. Heuristic reuse detection across 108 retrieval events shows high semantic relevance (mean embedding similarity 0.882) alongside variable structural proximity (mean code-fingerprint similarity 0.305), consistent with conceptual guidance rather than verbatim code copying.

</details>


### [254] [A Taxonomy of Runtime Faults in Model Context Protocol Servers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05339)
*Joshua Owotogbe,Indika Kumara,Willem-Jan van den Heuvel,Damian Andrew Tamburri,Antonio Ken Iannillo,Roberto Natella*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents a comprehensive empirical taxonomy of runtime faults in Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, identifying 11 categories and 27 subcategories from a detailed analysis of runtime faults.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address reliability challenges in tool-augmented AI workflows using MCP, especially those related to unexamined runtime fault characteristics.

Method: Manual analysis of 837 MCP-specific runtime fault threads from 473 GitHub repositories, followed by a bottom-up open coding procedure to categorize the faults.

Result: A taxonomy with 11 top-level categories and 27 subcategories of faults was developed, encompassing issues related to protocol interactions, tool invocations, and more, validated by surveys with MCP server developers.

Conclusion: The taxonomy accurately reflects observed runtime failures and is poised to aid in the maintenance and evolution of AI software using MCP.

Abstract: MCP (Model Context Protocol) enables LLMs (Large Language Models) to interact with external tools and data sources via a standardized protocol. Its rapid adoption in tool-augmented Artificial Intelligence (AI) workflows has introduced new reliability challenges, such as configuration parameters that are accepted but not enforced at runtime, leading to unintended default behavior, whose runtime fault characteristics remain empirically unexamined. We present the first empirical taxonomy of runtime faults in MCP servers. We manually analyzed 837 MCP-specific runtime fault threads from 473 actively maintained MCP server GitHub repositories and derived a taxonomy using a bottom-up open coding procedure. The taxonomy comprises 11 top-level categories and 27 subcategories (73 leaf fault types), covering recurrent failures across protocol interactions, tool invocations, schema enforcement, state management, model-provider integration, security validation, and timeouts or explicit cancellations of in-progress operations. To assess the taxonomy's external validity, we surveyed 55 MCP server developers. Respondents reported experiencing an average of 20 of the 27 fault subcategories, and no category remained unobserved. These results indicate that the taxonomy reflects widely observed runtime failures in MCP-based systems and shall assist AI software maintenance and evolution in the future.

</details>


### [255] [Human oversight of agentic systems in practice: Examining the oversight work, challenges, and heuristics of developers using software agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05391)
*Shipi Dhanorkar,Samir Passi,Mihaela Vorvoreanu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper explores the oversight dynamics in human-agent collaboration by studying developer practices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how developers oversee autonomous software agents in practice and identify the challenges they face.

Method: Conducting interviews with 17 experienced developers to explore their oversight strategies and challenges.

Result: Identified four forms of emergent oversight work: a priori control, co-planning, real-time monitoring, and post hoc review, highlighting reactive, preventative, and proactive oversight.

Conclusion: The findings inform human-centered design and software engineering practices, suggesting the need for enhanced support in agent oversight.

Abstract: Autonomous software agents hold promise to increase developer productivity but make mistakes and exhibit novel failure modes, making human oversight central to successful human-agent collaboration. Existing research on agent oversight is largely conceptual; normative frameworks exist, but how users actually oversee agents is less known. In this paper, we bridge this gap by providing early empirical anchors for the theoretical discourse on agent oversight. Drawing on interviews with 17 experienced developers, we conduct an exploratory inquiry examining what forms of emergent oversight work developers perform, when, and how. We also document the oversight challenges developers face and the strategies they have started using to address them. We found at least four forms of emergent oversight work: a priori control, co-planning, real-time monitoring, and post hoc review. We show that oversight work is not only reactive and retrospective, as portrayed in existing research, but also preventative and proactive. We describe situated oversight challenges (e.g., difficulty reviewing agent-generated code) and outline heuristics developers adopt to address such challenges (e.g., using test results as guarantees for code correctness). We conclude with high-level takeaways, future research directions, implications for the human-centered design of software agents and for software engineering practice, and limitations of our research.

</details>


### [256] [REStack: A Large-Scale Dataset of Reverse Engineering Discussions from Stack Exchange](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05493)
*Md Humaun Kabir,Md Rakibul Islam,Farha Kamal*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: REStack is a dataset comprising over 12,000 reverse engineering discussions from Stack Overflow and Reverse Engineering Stack Exchange, categorizing key topics and providing insights into practitioner challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the lack of empirical understanding of reverse engineering challenges and knowledge gaps in real-world settings, and to create a publicly available dataset of RE discussions.

Method: Dataset was created using Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) with Genetic Algorithm (GA)-based optimization for topic modeling, enhanced with metadata and difficulty indicators from community interactions.

Result: Identified 23 RE topics within six high-level categories, demonstrating that RE discussions are task-oriented, highlighting issues in debugging, decompilation, and more difficult topics like memory and firmware analysis.

Conclusion: REStack serves as a valuable resource for empirical studies, educational purposes, and enhances AI tools for developer assistance in reverse engineering, promoting reproducible research and data-driven practices.

Abstract: Reverse engineering (RE) is a critical activity in software engineering and cybersecurity, supporting tasks such as malware analysis, vulnerability discovery, legacy system maintenance, and firmware inspection. Despite its importance, there is limited empirical understanding of the challenges, topics, and knowledge gaps faced by RE practitioners in real-world settings, and no publicly available dataset has systematically captured RE discussions from developer Q&A forums.
  In this paper, we present REStack, a large-scale dataset of RE discussions collected from Stack Overflow and the dedicated Reverse Engineering Stack Exchange site. The dataset comprises over 12,000 RE-related posts spanning more than 15 years. Using Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) with Genetic Algorithm (GA)-based hyperparameter optimization, followed by manual topic labeling, we identify 23 semantically coherent RE topics grouped into six high-level thematic categories. The dataset is further enriched with metadata and difficulty indicators derived from community interaction signals, such as unanswered rates and response times.
  Our analysis reveals that RE discussions are predominantly practical and task-oriented, with strong emphasis on debugging, decompilation, and system-level analysis, while topics related to memory, firmware, and file format analysis exhibit high difficulty and unresolved rates. Beyond empirical characterization, REStack provides a reusable resource for empirical studies, educational research, and the development and evaluation of AI- and LLM-based developer assistance tools for RE. By releasing the dataset and accompanying scripts, this work aims to facilitate reproducible research and advance data-driven support for RE practice.

</details>


### [257] [STMutants: A Mutation Testing Dataset for Structured Text Programs in Industrial Automation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05499)
*Md Humaun Kabir,Md Rakibul Islam,Helen H. Lou*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper introduces STMutants, a publicly available dataset for mutation testing of IEC 61131-3 Structured Text programs, addressing a gap in research for this vital software used in industrial automation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The lack of a mutation testing benchmark for Structured Text (ST) programs is critical, given their use in safety-critical industrial applications where software faults can lead to severe consequences.

Method: The dataset was created by generating 110 first-order mutants from 11 ST programs, applying a four-phase methodology including fault profiling, transformation, verification, and manual screening.

Result: After screening, 108 mutants were retained, and three large language models demonstrated mutation detection accuracies of 86.1%, 94.4%, and 86.1%.

Conclusion: STMutants serves as the first public benchmark for ST programs, facilitating reproducible research in automated testing, mutation analysis, and quality assurance for PLC software.

Abstract: Mutation testing is widely used to evaluate test-suite effectiveness, yet IEC 61131-3 Structured Text (ST) programs still lack a publicly available benchmark that supports reproducible mutation-based research. This gap is especially important because ST is extensively used in Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) that operate in real-time, safety-critical industrial environments, where software faults may cause equipment damage, production loss, or unsafe system behavior. To address this need, we present STMutants, a curated mutation testing dataset for industrial automation software. STMutants contains 110 generated first-order mutants derived from 11 ST programs collected from the OSCAT basic library and industrially relevant sources, of which 108 are retained after observability and equivalence screening. The dataset covers seven mutation operator categories adapted from classical taxonomies for the PLC domain, including value, relational, arithmetic, logical, negation, operation insertion/omission, and initialization faults. Each mutant is constructed through a four-phase methodology: fault-type profiling and operator selection, syntactic transformation, compilability verification, and manual equivalence screening with strong inter-rater agreement (kappa = 0.87). To demonstrate the usefulness of the dataset, we evaluate three large language models (LLMs) in a two-phase setting: test-suite generation followed by mutation kill/survive prediction. Across 108 retained mutants, the models achieve mutation detection accuracies of 86.1%, 94.4%, and 86.1%, respectively, with statistical analysis confirming significant performance differences. By providing the first publicly available mutation benchmark for ST programs, STMutants enables reproducible research on automated test generation, mutation analysis, fault localization, and AI-assisted quality assurance for PLC software.

</details>


### [258] [From Failed Trajectories to Reliable LLM Agents: Diagnosing and Repairing Harness Flaws](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06324)
*Mengzhuo Chen,Junjie Wang,Zhe Liu,Yawen Wang,Qing Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: HarnessFix is a framework that enhances the reliability of LLM-based agents by diagnosing failures and repairing their execution harnesses through a trace-guided approach.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the limitations of existing self-improving agents that struggle to accurately locate and diagnose failures in execution environments, leading to inefficient and broad-spectrum solutions.

Method: HarnessFix compiles execution traces into a normalized representation (HTIR) to analyze failures at a granular level, attributing them to specific trajectory steps and harness layers, and generates targeted repair patches.

Result: HarnessFix demonstrates a performance improvement of 15.2% to 50% over original harnesses in various benchmarks, surpassing human-designed and self-evolution baselines while identifying recurring failure patterns.

Conclusion: The framework successfully improves agent performance and reliability by providing precise diagnostics and effective harness repairs.

Abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly rely on harnesses that provide execution environments, tool interfaces, context, lifecycle orchestration, observability, verification, and governance. Existing self-improving agents and automatic harness evolution methods mainly improve agents through runtime supervision, prompt optimization, workflow search, or harness modification based on final outcomes. However, they often fail to diagnose where the responsible evidence lies in failed trajectories and which harness layer causes the unreliable behavior, resulting in broad, indirect, or poorly scoped changes. This paper proposes HarnessFix, a trace-guided framework for diagnosing agent failures and repairing agent harnesses. HarnessFix compiles raw execution traces and harness code into a Harness-aware Trace Intermediate Representation (HTIR), which normalizes fragmented trajectory evidence and captures step-level provenance and control-flow relations. It then attributes failures to responsible trajectory steps and harness layers, consolidates recurring diagnoses into actionable flaw records, and maps them to scoped repair operators. Finally, HarnessFix generates and validates harness patches under flaw-specific repair specifications to reduce target flaws without introducing unacceptable regressions. We evaluate HarnessFix on SWE-Bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.0 Verified, GAIA and AppWorld. Across these benchmarks, HarnessFix improves held-out test performance over the initial harnesses by 15.2%--50.0%, outperforms human-designed and self-evolution baselines, and reveals recurring harness-flaw patterns across ETCLOVG layers.

</details>


### [259] [ADK Arena: Evaluating Agent Development Kits via LLM-as-a-Developer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05548)
*Jintao Huang,Xiaomin Li,Gaurav Mittal,Yu Hu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The study introduces a methodology, LLM-as-a-Developer, to evaluate the performance of various Agent Development Kits (ADKs) using an LLM. It finds that generation efforts indicate API usability, with varying costs and success rates across frameworks, emphasizing no framework's dominance and the substitutability of documentation and source knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To empirically assess how the choice of Agent Development Kit frameworks affects the performance of LLM-powered agents amidst the rapid development of these kits.

Method: Utilizing an LLM coding agent to learn APIs from documentation and iteratively write and repair code through validation feedback loops, conducted within an automated pipeline called ADK Arena.

Result: Out of 204 agent-benchmark pairs evaluated across 51 popular Python ADK frameworks, generation succeeds in 57% of cases; generation costs varied significantly across frameworks, indicating differing API complexities.

Conclusion: No framework consistently outperforms others; while the best frameworks can achieve high task resolution, many frameworks fail to reach even moderate success, and different types of knowledge (documentation, source code) largely provide similar utility.

Abstract: The rapid proliferation of Agent Development Kits (ADKs), SDK-level frameworks for building LLM-powered autonomous agents, has outpaced any empirical understanding of how framework choice affects agent performance. We propose \textbf{LLM-as-a-Developer}, a methodology that replaces human developers with an LLM coding agent that learns each framework's API from documentation, writes agent code, and iteratively repairs it through a validate-and-feedback loop until tests pass. By holding the developer constant and varying only the framework, generation effort becomes a quantitative proxy for API usability and the resulting agents provide a controlled measure of framework effectiveness. We implement this in \textbf{ADK Arena}, a fully automated pipeline with per-framework Docker isolation, a three-level validation pipeline, and benchmark adapters for SWE-bench, $τ^2$-bench, Terminal-Bench, and MCP-Atlas. Evaluating all 51 popular Python ADK frameworks (204 agent--benchmark pairs), we find that: (1)~generation succeeds for 57\% of runs, and its cost varies 5.6$\times$ across frameworks (\$0.6 to \$3.4 per agent), a quantitative proxy for API complexity, though cost alone does not predict success; (2)~no single framework dominates: the best single-benchmark ADK agents resolve up to 80\% of tasks and can even \emph{beat} general-purpose frontier coding agents at a fraction of the cost, yet the median framework resolves only 32\%; (3)~across information-source ablations, genuine framework usage stays within a narrow 28--40\% band (highest with raw source access and still 33\% with no reference material at all), indicating that documentation, source code, and parametric knowledge are largely substitutable rather than any one being a hard bottleneck.

</details>


### [260] [SmellBench: Towards Fine-Grained Evaluation of Code Agents on Refactoring Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05574)
*Fake Lin,Binbin Hu,Xi Zhu,Ziwei Zhao,Zhi Zheng,Ziqi Liu,Zhiqiang Zhang,Jun Zhou,Tong Xu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: SmellBench introduces a benchmark for evaluating code refactoring by injecting code smells into real-world code snippets, addressing the overlooked aspect of maintainability in code agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate code agents not just on functional correctness but also on the long-term maintainability of generated code.

Method: SmellBench injects code smells into clean code snippets sourced from real-world repositories, creating controlled refactoring cases across various difficulty levels and instruction settings.

Result: Tests reveal that existing agents struggle with a low elimination score of 50.34 for code smells, highlighting their limitations in understanding local versus cross-file issues.

Conclusion: The results indicate that enhancing agents' ability to tackle cross-file code smells is essential for improving overall refactoring quality.

Abstract: Code Agents have achieved remarkable advances in recent years, exhibiting strong capabilities across a wide range of software engineering tasks. However, their misuse often produces bloated and disorganized code that impairing readability, extensibility, and robustness. Despite this risk, existing benchmarks largely evaluate functional correctness rather than long-term maintainability of code agents. In this paper, we propose SmellBench, an extensible code refactoring benchmark that proactively injects code smells into clean code snippets from real-world repositories. This design enables the generation of controlled, high-quality, and diverse refactoring cases with human-written ground truth. Specifically, it contains 294 cases spanning 7 popular smell types, 3 difficulty levels, 2 instruction settings across 7 real-world repositories. We further design 3 evaluation aspects covering functional correctness, localization ability, and refactoring quality assessment. Experiments with 2 popular agents and 6 large langauge models (LLMs) show that the best combination - Qwen Code + Claude Sonnet 4.5 - achieved only a 50.34 score of smell elimination. Further analysis reveals that this gap arises from a focus on local code smells and a lack of cross-file understanding, which hinders comprehensive smell elimination.

</details>


### [261] [The End of Software Engineering: How AI Agents Are Fundamentally Restructuring the Software Paradigm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05608)
*Zhenfeng Cao*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper argues that AI agents, particularly using large language models (LLMs), signify a major shift in software engineering from static coding to dynamic, reasoning-driven code generation, introducing the concept of Agentic Engineering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the limitations of traditional software engineering as requirements evolve and to highlight the transformative potential of AI agents in this context.

Method: The authors conduct a first-principles analysis comparing traditional software with agentic systems and review historical transitions in software development models, alongside recent benchmark evidence.

Result: The analysis reveals significant differences in complexity management between traditional software and agentic systems, demonstrating both the advantages of the new paradigm and its challenges.

Conclusion: A four-stage roadmap is proposed for transitioning to self-evolving agent ecosystems, alongside practical recommendations for practitioners.

Abstract: For over half a century, software engineering has operated on a foundational premise: human engineers decompose problems, encode decision logic into static code, and manually adapt that code as requirements evolve. This paper argues that the emergence of AI agents -- systems where large language models serve as the primary reasoning engine, dynamically generating and discarding code as an instrumental resource -- constitutes not an incremental improvement but a fundamental restructuring of the software paradigm. Drawing on first-principles analysis of complexity scaling, we formalize the distinction between traditional software (where code is the carrier of decision logic) and agentic systems (where code is ephemeral tooling for an LLM-driven reasoning loop). We trace the historical arc from licensed software to SaaS to what we term Agent-as-a-Service (AaaS), showing that each shift transferred additional complexity away from end-users. We introduce the concept of Agentic Engineering as an emergent discipline -- distinct from software engineering in its core object of study, control model, and human role. Through analysis of recent benchmark evidence including SWE-bench Verified, EvoClaw, and LangChain's multi-agent coordination studies, we demonstrate both the transformative potential of the agentic paradigm and its current limitations. We conclude with a four-stage roadmap toward self-evolving agent ecosystems and concrete recommendations for practitioners navigating this transition.

</details>


### [262] [Enhancing Software Engineering Through Closed-Loop Memory Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05646)
*Xuehang Guo,Zora Zhiruo Wang,Qingyun Wang,Graham Neubig,Xingyao Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper introduces a framework for memory augmentation in software engineering agents, addressing issues with episodic memory and efficiency in task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current language models struggle with memory retention and reuse, hindering their performance across tasks.

Method: A closed-loop framework named \ours enhances memory utility by using validated downstream impact as an evaluation benchmark and optimization signal.

Result: The framework improves success rates by up to 5.25%, enhances resolve efficiency by up to 4.63%, and reduces computational costs by at least 9.79%.

Conclusion: \ours effectively addresses the limitations of episodic memory in SE agents, improving their performance and efficiency.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled powerful software engineering (SE) agents capable of navigating complex codebases and resolving real-world issues. However, these agents remain fundamentally episodic: they fail to retain, refine, and reuse experiences across tasks, repeatedly reconstructing context from scratch and reproducing similar mistakes. Even with memory support, they offer no remedy for the absence of a principled, task-agnostic \textit{memory utility}, making them difficult to evaluate rigorously or generalize across agents and settings. To tackle these limitations, we introduce \ours, a closed-loop framework for memory augmentation in SE agents. \ours grounds memory utility in \textit{validated downstream impact}, establishing utility as both a task-agnostic \textbf{evaluation benchmark} and an annotation-free \textbf{optimization signal}. Through complementary evaluation on \textit{single-episode} and \textit{cross-episode} memory augmentation, results demonstrate that \ours consistently improves SE agents across settings, achieving absolute gains of up to $\uparrow5.25\%$ in success rate and $\uparrow4.63\%$ in resolve efficiency, while substantially reducing computational cost by $\geq9.79\%$. Our project page: \href{https://xhguo7.github.io/MemOp/}{https://xhguo7.github.io/MemOp/}.

</details>


### [263] [When Surface Form Changes Moderation Decisions: A Paired Study of Code-Mixed Workflow Instability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05654)
*Suraj Babu Thimma Krishnaram*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This study evaluates hate moderation workflows on clean English versus Tamil-English code-mixed inputs, revealing significant discrepancies in action decisions and increased review burdens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To assess the reliability of hate moderation systems when faced with code-mixed language inputs compared to clean English.

Method: A paired evaluation approach was used, analyzing the same content in both clean English and Tamil-English code-mix, while measuring action decision stability and review rates.

Result: Code-mixed inputs showed a 26.5% flip rate in moderation decisions, increased review rates from 13.8% to 29.7%, and higher false flagging of non-hateful content, with Tamil-only inputs exhibiting even greater challenges.

Conclusion: Workflow evaluation exposes moderation issues that standard classification metrics might overlook, highlighting the need for improved language coverage and decision consistency.

Abstract: Hate moderation is often evaluated as classification on clean English inputs, but deployed systems must route content to actions such as ALLOW, FLAG, or REVIEW. We study how this workflow changes under code-mixed inputs using a paired evaluation setting where the same underlying content is expressed as clean English and Tamil-English code-mix. Under thresholds tuned on clean English development data, code-mixed inputs produce substantial action instability, with a paired clean- to-code-mix decision flip rate of 0.265. The main workflow effects are increased review burden and increased false-flagging of non-hateful content: review rate rises from 0.138 to 0.297 and non-hate false-flag rate rises from 0.069 to 0.104. Tamil-only inputs show stronger degradation overall, suggesting a broader language-coverage limitation rather than the same code-mixed instability pattern. A simple disagreement-based deferral rule reduces automatic errors on stressed inputs, but only by increasing review load. These results show that workflow-level evaluation reveals moderation failures that standard classification summaries can miss.

</details>


### [264] [Microskill Architecture: A Modular Skill-Driven Framework for AI-Native Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05720)
*Mohammad Zare,Omid Abdolrahmani*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: MicroSkill Architecture enhances AI-driven software development by using modular skill capsules to improve context management and efficiency, significantly reducing token consumption and increasing compilation success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses structural challenges in AI-native systems, particularly managing context windows during software development, to improve accuracy and efficiency.

Method: MicroSkill Architecture employs a modular design inspired by microservices, encapsulating knowledge into skill capsules and using a dynamic router for task-relevant selection. The context allocation is modeled as constrained optimization over semantic relevance within a token budget.

Result: An empirical case study demonstrated that MicroSkill reduces token consumption by over 90%, nearly doubles first-try compilation success rates, eliminates architectural violations, and facilitates autonomous creation of new skill capsules through self-learning.

Conclusion: MicroSkill Architecture presents a scalable solution for AI-native development systems, enhancing efficiency, reliability, and adaptability in software development.

Abstract: Large language models and AI coding agents have reshaped software development, but the path to fully AI-native systems faces structural challenges. Chief among them is managing context windows without losing accuracy or efficiency. When developers inject full project documentation and code into a model's memory, the model loses mid-sequence information, token costs spiral, and architecture drifts. This paper presents MicroSkill Architecture: a modular design paradigm inspired by microservices, applied to knowledge encapsulation instead of service decomposition. Instead of feeding an agent the entire codebase, the architecture partitions knowledge into atomic, sharply scoped skill capsules, and a dynamic router selects only semantically relevant capsules for the task. We formally model context allocation as constrained optimization over semantic relevance subject to a token budget. An empirical case study an enterprise content management system with fifteen complex features shows that MicroSkill cuts token consumption by over 90%, nearly doubles first-try compilation success rates, eliminates architectural violations entirely, and enables autonomous extraction and registration of seven new skill capsules via a self-learning mechanism. These findings suggest MicroSkill Architecture offers a scalable foundation for building AI-native development systems that are more efficient, more reliable, and capable of evolving over time.

</details>


### [265] [Human Oversight and Overload: Two Hidden and Costly Burdens of AI-Assisted Software Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05770)
*Vahid Garousi*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper examines the hidden burdens of AI in software engineering, focusing on the need for human oversight and the cognitive overload from AI-generated suggestions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate the often-overlooked challenges faced by software engineers when using AI tools and suggest how to address these issues.

Method: The study synthesizes practitioners' opinions and experiences to characterize the burdens imposed by AI technologies on software engineering tasks.

Result: Identified two primary burdens: the necessity of human oversight for AI outputs and the cognitive overload caused by numerous AI suggestions.

Conclusion: The paper emphasizes the importance of recognizing these challenges and encourages discussions on effective strategies for managing AI-related pressures in software engineering.

Abstract: AI is changing how software engineers work, but it often comes with hidden burdens and costs. In this paper, we characterize two such often-overlooked burdens: (1) the constant need for human oversight and inspection of AI-generated artifacts; and (2) the growing cognitive overload on software engineers from receiving large amounts of suggestions from AI tools. The need for human oversight is not optional-engineers must review, validate, and sometimes rework what AI produces. At the same time, the flood of AI suggestions, prompts, and possible solutions can leave developers mentally stretched. By blending evidence from recent opinions from practitioners, we highlight these often-overlooked challenges and open a conversation about how teams can handle them in day-to-day AI-assisted software engineering.

</details>


### [266] [Asuka-Bench: Benchmarking Code Agents on Underspecified User Intent and Multi-Round Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05920)
*Xin Wang,Liangtai Sun,Yaoming Zhu,Shuang Zhou,Jiaxing Liu,Fengjiao Chen,Lin Qiu,Xuezhi Cao,Xunliang Cai,Licheng Zhang,Zhendong Mao*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Asuka-Bench introduces a multi-round refinement benchmark for code generation that reflects real web development processes, evaluating models on their ability to respond to iterative feedback.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the mismatch between existing code-generation benchmarks and the iterative nature of real web development, where user intent clarifies over time.

Method: Asuka-Bench pairs underspecified user intent with multi-round refinement, utilizing a closed-loop system involving a Code Agent, UI Agent, and User LLM for evaluation and feedback.

Result: Benchmarking 8 LLMs across 50 web tasks revealed significant variability in Task Pass Rates, with a 38 percentage point difference and notable disparities in models' abilities to repair based on feedback.

Conclusion: The benchmark indicates substantial room for improvement, as even the best-performing model completed only 52% of projects after three rounds.

Abstract: Existing code-generation benchmarks score a single mapping from a complete prompt to a one-shot output. However, real web development is different. Users seldom write a full spec at the start; many requirements only become clear once they look at an intermediate result and react to it. We present Asuka-Bench, a benchmark that pairs underspecified user intent with multi-round refinement, grounded in browser-rendered behavior. Each task is resolved through a closed loop: a Code Agent generates a web project, a UI Agent executes test cases on the deployed site, and a User LLM turns evaluation outcomes into natural-language feedback for the next round. The benchmark comprises 50 web tasks with 784 evaluation criteria and 2402 expected outcomes. We benchmark 8 LLMs across 2 agent frameworks. The results separate models clearly: weighted Task Pass Rate varies by 38 percentage points and models also differ substantially in their ability to repair from feedback. Asuka-Bench is also far from saturated: even the strongest model completes only 52% of projects after three rounds.

</details>


### [267] [Metamorphic Testing with the Rashomon Set: Explanation Faithfulness in Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06056)
*Helge Spieker,Jørn Eirik Betten,Arnaud Gotlieb*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents a framework for assessing the trustworthiness of explanations in machine learning models, tackling the Rashomon effect through metamorphic testing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The study addresses the Rashomon effect in machine learning, which highlights the challenge of determining trustworthy explanations from models that perform similarly.

Method: A novel framework is proposed that utilizes metamorphic testing to evaluate explanation faithfulness by examining feature importance from post-hoc explanation methods without needing ground-truth labels.

Result: The framework features five metamorphic relations that outline expected consistency between model behavior and feature attributions, and it was applied to two regression datasets and two post-hoc methods (SHAP and LIME).

Conclusion: This model-agnostic framework serves as an effective tool for identifying accurate models paired with reliable explanations.

Abstract: Multiple machine learning models can achieve near-equivalent predictive performance on the same task, yet provide divergent feature-based explanations. This is called the Rashomon effect of (explainable) machine learning, and it raises the question of which explanations, if any, are trustworthy. We propose a framework based on metamorphic testing that assesses explanation faithfulness without requiring ground-truth labels by exploring attributed feature importance from post-hoc explanation methods. Five metamorphic relations formalize expected consistency properties between model behavior and feature attributions. We apply this general framework to two tabular regression datasets and two post-hoc explainers (SHAP and LIME) to demonstrate the approach. The framework offers a practical, model-agnostic tool for selecting accurate models with reliable and trustworthy explanations.

</details>


### [268] [TLA-Prover: Verifiable TLA+ Specification Synthesis via Preference-Optimized Low-Rank Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06133)
*Eric Spencer,Arslan Bisharat,Brian Ortiz,Khushboo Bhadauria,TaiNing Wang,George K. Thiruvathukal,Konstantin Laufer,Mohammed Abuhamad*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: TLA-Prover is a large language model designed to improve the synthesis of TLA+ specifications by using supervised fine-tuning and a repair-based optimization method, achieving significant improvements over existing baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enhance the precision of TLA+ specifications generated by LLMs and address the high failure rates in model checking.

Method: Utilizes supervised fine-tuning on verified examples and repair-based group-relative policy optimization to enhance specification synthesis, along with a direct preference optimization variant for comparison.

Result: TLA-Prover achieves a pass rate of 30% at Gold and Diamond on a benchmark, significantly outperforming the untuned baseline.

Conclusion: The approach demonstrates effective enhancement in TLA+ specification correctness through innovative training methods, marking an advancement in the field.

Abstract: TLA+ is a formal specification language for verifying distributed systems and safety-critical protocols. Large language models (LLMs) frequently produce TLA+ specifications that fail the TLC model checker for semantic reasons. Across 25 LLMs, the best public baseline is 26.6% syntactic parse and 8.6% semantic model-check. We present TLA-Prover, a 20-billion-parameter model for TLA+ specification synthesis. Training combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on verified examples with repair-based group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). In the GRPO stage, the model learns to fix its own rejected specifications. We also train a direct preference optimization (DPO) variant from the same SFT checkpoint as an ablation. TLC provides the reward signal directly, with no learned reward model. Four tiers grade each output: Bronze (parses), Silver (no warnings), Gold (passes TLC), and Diamond. To reach Diamond, the model's correctness property is automatically altered in a small way; TLC must then detect a violation. If TLC still passes, the property was always-true and contributes nothing; the output fails Diamond. TLA-Prover reaches 9/30 (i.e. pass@1 = 30%) at both Gold and Diamond on a held-out 30-problem benchmark. This is roughly 3.5x the 8.6% untuned baseline. The DPO variant reaches 20% at Diamond. Gold and Diamond coincide at every checkpoint; this prevents the trivial-property failure mode.

</details>


### [269] [Towards the Readability of LLM-Generated Codes through Multitask Representation Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06214)
*Huifan Gao,Liuhua He,Yinghui Pan,Shenbao Yu,Yifeng Zeng,Shengchao Qin,Weidi Sun*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes a multitask representation engineering framework to enhance code readability in LLM-generated code while addressing the tradeoff with correctness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need to improve code readability in addition to correctness for enhancing overall code quality.

Method: The paper employs a multitask representation engineering (RepE) framework to manage control over multiple tasks for improving code readability.

Result: Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the multitask RepE framework in balancing code readability and correctness.

Conclusion: The multitask approach to representation engineering is essential for addressing the subjective nature of code readability while maintaining functional fidelity.

Abstract: Correctness and readability are key measures of code quality, respectively ensuring functional fidelity and ease of comprehension. While most existing research focuses on improving the correctness of large language models~(LLMs) generated codes, readability remains under-addressed. Enhancing readability through targeted control is challenging due to its subjective nature. In this article, we employ representation engineering~(RepE) as the targeted control method given its characteristics of low data dependency and low computational cost. Prior work on RepE has primarily focused on the targeted control for a single task, but improving the code readability requires the control across multiple tasks. Accordingly we proposes the multitask RepE framework and theoretically discuss the impact of the multitask steering method on the tradeoff between the code readability and correctness. We further provide comprehensive experiments in support. All the relevant implementations are open-source and available upon request.

</details>


### [270] [Domain Diversity, Motivation, Inclusion, and Feedback in Software Modelling Education](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06275)
*Isabella Graßl,Christopher Lazik,Shalini Chakraborty,Grischa Liebel,Miguel Goulão*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Research investigates the impact of problem domain choices on student engagement in software modelling education, highlighting a disconnect between educator assumptions and student preferences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of fostering motivation and inclusivity in software modelling education, an area that has been underexplored compared to tools and assessments.

Method: The study involved parallel surveys conducted with 90 students and 22 educators to assess preferences and perceptions regarding problem domains in modelling education.

Result: Findings indicate that students are more motivated by socially relevant problem domains and prefer having a choice, while educators tend to overestimate interest in traditional study-related domains.

Conclusion: The research emphasizes the importance of inclusive domain selection to enhance student motivation and engagement, recommending a shift towards student-centred approaches in domain selection.

Abstract: Student engagement is critical for effective learning in software modelling, yet fostering motivation and inclusivity remains a challenge. While existing research has focused on modelling tools, notations, and assessment, little attention has been given to how the choice of problem domains and the diversity, relatability, and cultural perspectives they bring shape students' learning experiences. This study explores how problem domains and teaching methods influence motivation, engagement, inclusiveness, and feedback in modelling education. To investigate these dimensions, we conducted parallel surveys with 90 students and 22 educators. Our findings reveal disconnects between educator assumptions and student preferences: Students show greatest motivation for socially relevant domains and prefer choice in selection, while educators overestimate interest in study-related domains. The study identifies how minor design choices can exclude students. Students perceive feedback as meaningful when visibly acted upon. These findings suggest inclusive domain selection is central to student motivation; thus, we recommend student-centred domain selection.

</details>


### [271] [More than a Judge: An Empirical Study of Agent-Human Interaction in Crowdsourced Testing Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06301)
*Yue Wang,Yuan Zhao,Shengcheng Yu,Zhenyu Chen,Qing Gu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates the impact of agentic AI feedback on improving report quality in crowdsourced testing, demonstrating that such feedback enhances revisions and overall task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The integration of agentic AI into software engineering aims to alleviate the review burden caused by varied quality in crowdsourced testing reports.

Method: A controlled four-stage human-subject study was conducted with 20 testers using real-world applications to evaluate the effects of assessment-derived feedback on report revisions and performance.

Result: Agent-generated feedback led to immediate improvements in revised reports, enhanced performance on new tasks, and evidence of meaningful transfer of practices across applications.

Conclusion: The study provides empirical evidence that assessment agents can function as effective feedback providers within workflow, improving report quality in crowdsourced testing.

Abstract: Agentic AI is increasingly being integrated into software engineering workflows. In crowdsourced testing, however, the large volume and uneven quality of submitted reports still create a substantial review burden for developers. In prior work, we developed and validated a multi-agent assessment backbone based on the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm. That backbone assesses reports along three dimensions--textuality, adequacy, and competitiveness--and was shown to align well with human consensus while substantially reducing assessment effort. Yet reliable automated judging does not by itself show whether agent outputs can improve human work when embedded into workflow. This paper studies that missing question in the context of crowdsourced testing. We investigate whether assessment-derived, actionable feedback can improve how testers revise reports, perform on later tasks, and transfer reporting practices across applications. To do so, we conducted a controlled four-stage human-subject study with 20 testers across three real-world applications. The results show that agent-generated feedback supports immediate improvements in revised reports, better first submissions on a new task after prior feedback exposure, and evidence of partial but meaningful transfer to a later application. A post-task questionnaire completed by 17 participants complements these artifact-based findings by suggesting that the feedback was generally understandable, acted upon in revision, and carried into later tasks, while also revealing remaining friction in specificity and execution. Overall, the study provides empirical evidence that, in the studied crowdsourced testing setting, assessment agents can serve not only as post-hoc judges but also as workflow-integrated feedback providers that support upstream report-quality improvement.

</details>


### [272] [Scaffold, Not Vocabulary? A Controlled, Two-Tier, Pre-Registered Study of a Popperian Code-Generation Skill](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06454)
*Mehmet Iscan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The study examines the effectiveness of prompt skills in large language models, specifically looking at whether improvements in code generation come from Popperian methodology or scaffold structure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine if the observed gains in code generation by large language models stem from the use of Popperian falsificationist prompts or the structure provided by the scaffolding.

Method: The authors conducted a two-tier ablation study with different control groups, including a placebo and a labels-only scaffold, on two models (Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B) to assess performance improvements in code generation.

Result: On the Claude model, no significant improvement was observed; on the Qwen model, structured scaffolding showed better performance, but the Popperian skill did not provide additional benefits over a labels-only scaffold.

Conclusion: The study concludes that the perceived improvements in code generation are primarily due to scaffold structure rather than the Popperian content's procedural approach.
